### Inter-State and International Borders | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/assam-geography-sec/borders-interstate-international-assam/
Summary: Important questions on the inter-state and international borders of Assam for competitive exams. Covers ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: Which country shares the international border with Assam?
A: Bhutan and Bangladesh.
Q: Which state of India shares its border with Assam?
A: Seven states: Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram and West Bengal.
Q: Which district of Assam shares the international border with Bhutan?
A: Kokrajhar, Chirang, Baksa, Udalguri, Darrang, Sonitpur and Bishwanath districts.
Q: Which district of Assam shares the border with Bangladesh?
A: Dhubri and Karimganj districts.
Q: Which district of Assam shares its border with Arunachal Pradesh?
A: Tinsukia, Dibrugarh, Lakhimpur, Dhemaji, Sonitpur, Biswanath and Baksa districts.
Q: Which district of Assam shares its border with Nagaland?
A: Golaghat, Jorhat, Sivasagar and Charaideo districts.
Q: Which district of Assam shares its border with Manipur?
A: Cachar and Hailakandi districts.
Q: Which district of Assam shares its border with Meghalaya?
A: Kamrup, Goalpara, Karbi Anglong, Dima Hasao, Cachar, Karimganj and West Karbi Anglong.
Q: Which district of Assam shares its border with Tripura?
A: Hailakandi district.
Q: Which district of Assam shares its border with Mizoram?
A: Cachar, Hailakandi and Karimganj districts.
Q: Which district of Assam shares its border with West Bengal?
A: Kokrajhar, Dhubri and Chirang districts.
Q: Which is the longest inter-state border of Assam?
A: The border with Arunachal Pradesh is the longest.
Q: What is the total length of the international border of Assam?
A: About 288 kilometres with Bhutan and Bangladesh.
Q: What is the length of the Assam-Bhutan border?
A: About 267 kilometres.
Q: What is the length of the Assam-Bangladesh border?
A: About 21 to 22 kilometres.
Q: Which river forms a part of the border between Assam and Meghalaya?
A: The Simsang river and parts of the Kopili river area.
Q: Which river separates Assam from Arunachal Pradesh in some parts?
A: The Brahmaputra and its tributaries like the Siang and the Dibang areas.
Q: Which is the main border town of Assam on the Bhutan border?
A: Samdrup Jongkhar is on the Bhutan side, and the Assam side has Darrang's border areas.
Q: Which is the main land customs station of Assam on the Bangladesh border?
A: The Karimganj land customs station.
Q: Which river separates Assam from Bangladesh in the Dhubri area?
A: The Brahmaputra (Jamuna) river in the Dhubri area.
Q: Which pass connects Assam with Bhutan?
A: The passes of the Bhutan hills in the north, like the Buxa area route.
Q: Which is the border district of Assam on the south-west side?
A: Kokrajhar and Dhubri districts.
Q: Which river flows into Bangladesh from the Barak valley of Assam?
A: The Barak river, which becomes the Surma and later the Meghna.
Q: Which is the easternmost point of the border of Assam?
A: The Sadiya region in Tinsukia district.
Q: Which district of Assam is surrounded by other states?
A: Karimganj is surrounded by Bangladesh, Tripura and Mizoram on most sides.
Q: Which is the westernmost border point of Assam?
A: The Dhubri area on the West Bengal and Bangladesh border.

### Brahmaputra and Barak Valley | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/assam-geography-sec/brahmaputra-barak-valley/
Summary: Important questions on the Brahmaputra and Barak river systems and valleys of Assam for competitive exams. Relevant for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other government exams.
Q: Where does the Brahmaputra river originate?
A: From the Chemayungdung glacier in the Kailash range of the Himalayas in Tibet.
Q: What is the Tibetan name of the Brahmaputra river?
A: Tsangpo (Yarlung Tsangpo).
Q: Through which mountain range does the Brahmaputra enter India?
A: The Eastern Himalayas, near Sadiya in Arunachal Pradesh.
Q: What is the name of the Brahmaputra after it enters Arunachal Pradesh?
A: Siang (Dihang).
Q: What is the total length of the Brahmaputra river?
A: About 2,900 km, of which about 900 km flows through Assam.
Q: Which is the largest river valley in Assam?
A: The Brahmaputra valley.
Q: Where does the Brahmaputra enter Bangladesh?
A: Near Dhubri in Assam, after which it is known as the Jamuna in Bangladesh.
Q: Where does the Brahmaputra finally meet the sea?
A: It merges with the Ganga (Padma) and the Meghna before falling into the Bay of Bengal.
Q: Where does the Barak river originate?
A: From the hills of Manipur.
Q: Which is the largest river of the Barak valley?
A: The Barak river.
Q: Which districts are part of the Barak valley?
A: Cachar, Karimganj and Hailakandi.
Q: What is the Barak river known as in Bangladesh?
A: It splits into the Surma and the Kushiyara.
Q: Which is the only major tributary joining the Brahmaputra from the south in the lower reaches?
A: The Manas river.
Q: What type of river is the Brahmaputra in terms of flow?
A: It is a braided river with a large number of channels and sandbars.
Q: Which is the largest river island in the world located in Assam?
A: Majuli, formed by the Brahmaputra river.
Q: What is the characteristic feature of the Brahmaputra's north bank?
A: Steeper slopes and erosion, with fewer tributaries from the north.
Q: Which is the main river system of South Assam?
A: The Barak river system.
Q: What is the annual flood problem mainly caused by in Assam?
A: The heavy monsoon discharge of the Brahmaputra and its tributaries.
Q: Which valley is known as the tea valley of Assam?
A: The Brahmaputra valley, especially the upper Assam region.
Q: Which river is called the 'sorrow of Assam'?
A: The Brahmaputra, due to its frequent devastating floods.
Q: Which is the longest bridge over the Brahmaputra in Assam?
A: The Bhupen Hazarika Setu (Dhola-Sadiya bridge).
Q: Which tributary of the Brahmaputra is known as the 'Lohit'?
A: The Lohit river, a major tributary joining from Arunachal Pradesh.
Q: What is the average width of the Brahmaputra in Assam?
A: It ranges from about 1 km to 18 km in different stretches.
Q: Which is the deepest point of the Brahmaputra?
A: Near Sadiya, where the depth exceeds 38 metres at some places.
Q: Which are the major tributaries of the Brahmaputra from the north?
A: Subansiri, Siang, Dibang, Lohit, Dhansiri (north) and Sankosh.
Q: What is the name of the Brahmaputra before it enters India?
A: Yarlung Tsangpo (in Tibet).
Q: Is Brahmaputra and Barak Valley available for free on axomexam?
A: Yes. All questions, answers and explanations for Brahmaputra and Barak Valley are completely free, with no login or payment required.

A: Yes. Every question and answer in this topic is bilingual, so you can practise in Assamese and English.

### Climate, Monsoon and Floods | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/assam-geography-sec/climate-monsoon-floods-assam/
Summary: Important questions on the climate, monsoon and flood problems of Assam for competitive exams. Practice for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What type of climate does Assam have?
A: A humid subtropical climate with heavy rainfall.
Q: What is the average annual rainfall of Assam?
A: About 2,500 mm to 3,000 mm.
Q: Which is the wettest place in Assam?
A: Mawsynram in Meghalaya is the wettest overall, but in Assam the northern districts receive high rainfall.
Q: Which monsoon brings most of the rainfall to Assam?
A: The South-West monsoon.
Q: During which months does Assam receive the maximum rainfall?
A: June to September.
Q: What is the average temperature of Assam in summer?
A: About 25°C to 32°C.
Q: What is the average winter temperature of Assam?
A: About 10°C to 15°C.
Q: Which are the main seasons of Assam?
A: Winter, Pre-monsoon, Monsoon and Retreating monsoon.
Q: What is the 'Kalbaisakhi' or 'Bordoisila'?
A: The local thunderstorm which occurs in the pre-monsoon season (April-May) in Assam.
Q: What is the main cause of the floods in Assam?
A: The heavy monsoon rainfall and the siltation of the Brahmaputra and its tributaries.
Q: How many times in a year does Assam generally experience floods?
A: Generally two to three waves of floods during the monsoon season.
Q: Which is the flood-prone district of Assam?
A: Most districts of the Brahmaputra valley, especially Morigaon, Nagaon, Barpeta and Dhubri, are flood-prone.
Q: Which organization manages the flood control in Assam?
A: The Brahmaputra Board and the Assam State Disaster Management Authority (ASDMA).
Q: What is the Brahmaputra Board?
A: A statutory body set up in 1980 for the planning of flood control and development of the Brahmaputra valley.
Q: What is the effect of floods on the agriculture of Assam?
A: It damages the paddy crops and reduces agricultural productivity.
Q: What is the annual loss caused by floods in Assam estimated at?
A: The floods cause enormous losses of life, property and crops every year.
Q: Which wind is responsible for the heavy rainfall of Assam?
A: The moisture-laden south-west monsoon winds from the Bay of Bengal.
Q: What is the average humidity of Assam?
A: It is high throughout the year, ranging between 70% and 90%.
Q: Which is the coldest region of Assam?
A: The hill district of Dima Hasao (North Cachar Hills).
Q: What is the main source of the monsoon rainfall of Assam?
A: The Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea branches of the south-west monsoon.
Q: Which place of Assam receives the highest rainfall?
A: The northern districts like Lakhimpur and Dhemaji receive very high rainfall.
Q: What is the effect of the retreating monsoon on Assam?
A: It brings light rainfall and the onset of the winter season.
Q: Which river system is responsible for the floods in the Barak valley?
A: The Barak river and its tributaries.
Q: What is the role of embankments in flood control in Assam?
A: They are constructed along the rivers to prevent the water from overflowing, though they often breach.
Q: Which is the largest river of Assam responsible for most of its floods?
A: The Brahmaputra.
Q: What is the percentage of Assam's area that is flood-prone?
A: About 40% of the area of Assam is flood-prone.

A: Yes. All questions, answers and explanations for Climate, Monsoon and Floods are completely free, with no login or payment required.

A: Yes. Every question and answer in this topic is bilingual, so you can practise in Assamese and English.

### Forest Types and Area | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/assam-geography-sec/forest-types-area-assam/
Summary: Important questions on the types and area of forests in Assam for competitive exams. Covers ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What percentage of Assam's total geographical area is covered by forest?
A: About 35% to 36% is under forest and tree cover.
Q: Which type of forest covers the largest area in Assam?
A: Tropical wet evergreen forests and tropical moist deciduous forests.
Q: Which forests are found in the lower reaches of the Brahmaputra valley?
A: Tropical moist deciduous and semi-evergreen forests.
Q: Which type of forest is found in the upper reaches of the Brahmaputra valley?
A: Tropical wet evergreen forests.
Q: Which forests are found in the hill districts of Karbi Anglong and Dima Hasao?
A: Subtropical evergreen and montane (temperate) forests.
Q: Which is the main forest type of the Barak valley?
A: Tropical wet evergreen and semi-evergreen forests.
Q: Which trees are found in the tropical wet evergreen forests of Assam?
A: Hollong, Nahor, Ajhar, Mekang and Nahar trees.
Q: Which is the tallest tree of the Assam rainforest?
A: The Hollong tree (Dipterocarpus macrocarpus).
Q: What are the grassland areas of Assam called?
A: They are called 'khayer' or floodplain grasslands, like those of Kaziranga.
Q: Which is the largest forest division of Assam?
A: The Karbi Anglong forest division is among the largest in area.
Q: What is the total recorded forest area of Assam?
A: About 26,000 to 27,000 square kilometres.
Q: Which forest type covers the Kaziranga National Park?
A: Tropical moist deciduous forests and alluvial grasslands.
Q: Which bamboo species is abundant in the forests of Assam?
A: Muli (Melocanna) and Jati (Bambusa) bamboo species.
Q: Which sanctuary of Assam is known for its semi-evergreen forests?
A: The Nameri and the Dibru-Saikhowa sanctuaries have semi-evergreen forests.
Q: What is the main forest product of the forests of Assam?
A: Timber, bamboo and cane.
Q: Which is the main timber tree of the tropical moist deciduous forests of Assam?
A: Sal (Shorea robusta) and Teak.
Q: What is the 'reserved forest' in Assam?
A: A forest notified for protection and conservation under the Forest Act.
Q: Which district has the highest forest cover in Assam?
A: Karbi Anglong has the highest forest cover.
Q: Which type of forest is found along the river banks of the Brahmaputra?
A: Riverine (riparian) forests and grasslands.
Q: What is the main vegetation of the Manas National Park?
A: Tropical moist deciduous forests, alluvial grasslands and bamboo forests.
Q: Which rare tree is found in the Dehing-Patkai rainforest?
A: The Hollong, and the giant tree species of the lowland evergreen forests.
Q: What is the trend of the forest cover in Assam in recent years?
A: There has been a slight decrease in dense forest cover but an increase in open forest cover.
Q: Which forest is famous for the 'Sal' trees in Assam?
A: The Sal forests of the western districts like the Nameri area and the lower Brahmaputra region.
Q: Which is the main cause of the depletion of forests in Assam?
A: Jhum cultivation, illegal felling, encroachment and floods.
Q: What is the forest cover percentage of Assam as per the latest State of Forest Report?
A: About 36% of the geographical area is under forest cover.
Q: Which tree species is found in the subtropical forests of the Barail range?
A: Species like the Nahor, the Ajar and the Orchid-bearing trees of the moist forests.

Q: What is the highest peak of the Karbi Anglong hills?
A: Singhasan (Dhengdhenjan) peak, about 1,360 metres high.
Q: Which hill range lies between the Brahmaputra valley and the Barak valley?

Q: Which is the only hill station of Assam?

A: The Barak river and several of its tributaries.

A: The Rongker festival.

URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/assam-geography-sec/minerals-oil-gas-coal-limestone/

Q: Which district is the largest producer of oil in Assam?

Q: Where is the biggest gas processing plant of Assam located?
A: At Duliajan.
Q: Which is the main coal producing district of Assam?
A: Tinsukia district (at Ledo, Margherita and Tipong).

Q: Which is the largest gas field of Assam?
A: The Lakwa gas field in Sivasagar district.
Q: What is natural gas mainly used for in Assam?
A: For power generation, fertilizer production and as feedstock for petrochemical industries.
Q: Where is the Assam Gas Cracker Project located?
A: At Lepetkata, near Dibrugarh.
Q: Which company operates the Assam Gas Cracker Project?
A: Brahmaputra Cracker and Polymer Limited (BCPL).
Q: Which minerals other than coal are found in Assam?
A: Limestone, crude oil, natural gas, silica sand and minor minerals.
Q: Which is the main petrochemical hub of Assam?
A: Duliajan and the Dibrugarh region.
Q: Which is the main oil bearing area of the Barak valley?
A: The Badarpur and Patharia areas of Karimganj.
Q: What is the total crude oil production of Assam?
A: Assam produces about 3 million tonnes of crude oil annually.
Q: Which is the oldest refinery of Assam after Digboi?
A: The Guwahati refinery, established in 1962.
Q: Which district of Assam is famous for the 'coal city'?
A: Tinsukia, especially Margherita, known for its coal mines.

A: Pobitora Wildlife Sanctuary in Marigaon district.

### Ramsar Sites and Endemic Flora, Fauna | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/assam-geography-sec/ramsar-endemic-flora-fauna-assam/
Summary: Important questions on the Ramsar sites and endemic flora and fauna of Assam for competitive exams. Practice for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What is a Ramsar site?
A: A wetland site designated under the Ramsar Convention for its international importance.
Q: Where was the Ramsar Convention held?

A: In 1975.

A: The greater adjutant stork and the Bengal florican.

A: The one-horned rhinoceros.
Q: Which is the state bird of Assam?
A: The white-winged wood duck (Deo Hah).
Q: Which is the state tree of Assam?
A: The Hollong tree (Dipterocarpus macrocarpus).
Q: Which is the state flower of Assam?
A: The Fox tail orchid (Kopou phool - Rhynchostylis retusa).
Q: Which animal is endemic to the Brahmaputra river?
A: The Ganges river dolphin (susuk).

Q: Which endemic fish species is found in the rivers of Assam?
A: The pabho (Gudusia chapra), chital and the famous 'Na-mach' or the hilsa-like riverine species.
Q: Which plant is used traditionally in Assam for making 'gamosa'?
A: Cotton is used, while the endi, muga and pat silks come from silkworms feeding on specific plants.
Q: Which rare orchid is found in the forests of Assam?
A: The Vanda coerulea (blue orchid) and Rhynchostylis retusa (Kopou).
Q: Which is the most important endemic mammal of the Kaziranga National Park?
A: The Indian one-horned rhinoceros.
Q: Which termite-resistant timber tree is endemic to Assam's forests?
A: The Hollong tree, which is the tallest tree of Assam's rainforests.
Q: Which butterfly species endemic to Assam is protected?
A: The golden birdwing and the Kaiser-i-hind are found in the forests of Assam.
Q: What is the main threat to the endemic species of Assam?
A: Habitat loss due to floods, deforestation and encroachment.

### Tiger Reserves and Biosphere Reserve | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/assam-geography-sec/tiger-biosphere-reserves-assam/
Summary: Important questions on the tiger reserves and biosphere reserves of Assam for competitive exams. Practice for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: How many tiger reserves are there in Assam?
A: Four tiger reserves.
Q: Which are the tiger reserves of Assam?
A: Manas, Nameri, Orang and Dehing-Patkai tiger reserves.
Q: When was the Manas National Park declared a tiger reserve?
A: In 1973-74, under Project Tiger.
Q: When was Nameri declared a tiger reserve?
A: In 2000.
Q: When was the Orang tiger reserve declared?
A: In 2016.
Q: When was the Dehing-Patkai tiger reserve declared?
A: In 2020.
Q: In which district is the Dehing-Patkai tiger reserve located?
A: Tinsukia and Dibrugarh districts.
Q: What is the river associated with the Manas tiger reserve?
A: The Manas river.
Q: What is the river associated with Nameri tiger reserve?
A: The Jia-Bhoroli (Kameng) river.
Q: Which biosphere reserve is present in Assam?
A: The Manas biosphere reserve (shared with the Manas National Park).
Q: In which year was the Manas biosphere reserve declared?
A: In 1989.
Q: What is the core area of the Manas biosphere reserve?
A: The Manas National Park.
Q: Which species is the key protected animal of the Nameri tiger reserve?
A: The royal Bengal tiger.
Q: What is Project Tiger?
A: A national programme launched in 1973 for the conservation of tigers and their habitats.
Q: What is the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA)?
A: A statutory body set up in 2005 to oversee the management of tiger reserves in India.
Q: Which is the largest tiger reserve of Assam by area?
A: Manas tiger reserve.

Q: Which river is a tributary of the Barak river?

### Dwarf Planets, Asteroids, Comets & Meteors | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/astronomical-geography-sec/dwarf-planets-asteroids-comets-meteors/
Summary: Important questions on dwarf planets, asteroids, comets and meteors for competitive exams. Practice for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What is a dwarf planet?
A: A dwarf planet is a celestial body that orbits the Sun, has enough mass for a round shape, but has not cleared its orbit of other objects.
Q: Who defined the term 'dwarf planet'?
A: The International Astronomical Union (IAU) defined the term 'dwarf planet' in 2006.
Q: Name the five recognized dwarf planets.
A: The five recognized dwarf planets are Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, and Eris.
Q: Where is Pluto located?
A: Pluto is located in the Kuiper Belt, a region beyond Neptune's orbit.
Q: When was Pluto reclassified from a planet to a dwarf planet?
A: Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 by the IAU.
Q: Who discovered Pluto?
A: Pluto was discovered by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930.
Q: What is the Kuiper Belt?
A: The Kuiper Belt is a disc-shaped region beyond Neptune's orbit containing icy bodies, dwarf planets, and short-period comets.
Q: What is an asteroid?
A: An asteroid is a small rocky body that orbits the Sun, mainly found in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
Q: What is the largest asteroid?
A: Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt, so large that it is classified as a dwarf planet.
Q: What is a comet?
A: A comet is an icy body that, when near the Sun, develops a glowing coma and tail from evaporating ice and dust.
Q: What are the parts of a comet?
A: A comet consists of a nucleus, coma, hydrogen envelope, and two tails - the dust tail and ion tail.
Q: What is Halley's Comet's orbital period?
A: Halley's Comet has an orbital period of about 76 years.
Q: Where do long-period comets come from?
A: Long-period comets are believed to come from the Oort Cloud, a distant spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the solar system.
Q: What is the difference between a meteoroid, meteor, and meteorite?
A: A meteoroid is a small rock in space; a meteor is the streak of light when it burns in the atmosphere; a meteorite is the piece that survives and lands on Earth.
Q: What is a meteor shower?
A: A meteor shower occurs when Earth passes through the debris trail left by a comet, causing many meteors to appear.
Q: What is the Perseid meteor shower associated with?
A: The Perseid meteor shower is associated with comet Swift-Tuttle.
Q: What is the Oort Cloud?
A: The Oort Cloud is a hypothesized spherical cloud of icy objects surrounding the solar system, the source of long-period comets.
Q: What is Eris?
A: Eris is a dwarf planet in the scattered disc beyond the Kuiper Belt, and is the most massive known dwarf planet.
Q: What is Ceres?
A: Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt and the only dwarf planet located in the inner solar system.
Q: What is a near-Earth object (NEO)?
A: A near-Earth object is an asteroid or comet whose orbit brings it close to Earth's orbit.
Q: What is a fireball?
A: A fireball is an unusually bright meteor, brighter than Venus, that explodes or streaks across the sky.
Q: What is the Chicxulub crater linked to?
A: The Chicxulub crater in Mexico is linked to the asteroid impact that is believed to have caused the extinction of the dinosaurs about 66 million years ago.
Q: What are the names of the inner and outer asteroid zones?
A: The main asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter, and the Trojan asteroids share Jupiter's orbit; the Kuiper Belt lies beyond Neptune.
Q: What is the Tunguska event?
A: The Tunguska event was a massive explosion in Siberia in 1908, believed to be caused by an asteroid or comet airburst.
Q: What is the difference between an asteroid and a comet?
A: An asteroid is mostly rocky and found in the inner solar system, while a comet is mostly icy and develops a tail when near the Sun.

A: Yes. All questions, answers and explanations for Dwarf Planets, Asteroids, Comets & Meteors are completely free, with no login or payment required.

### Earth: Rotation, Revolution, Inclination & Seasons | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/astronomical-geography-sec/earth-rotation-revolution-seasons/
Summary: Important questions on Earth's rotation, revolution, axial inclination and seasons for competitive exams. Practice for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What is the rotation of the Earth?
A: Rotation is the spinning of Earth on its own axis from west to east, which causes day and night.
Q: How long does the Earth take to complete one rotation?
A: Earth takes about 24 hours (23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds) to complete one rotation on its axis.
Q: What is the revolution of the Earth?
A: Revolution is the movement of Earth around the Sun in its elliptical orbit, which causes the change of seasons.
Q: How long does the Earth take to complete one revolution around the Sun?
A: Earth takes about 365.25 days (one year) to complete one revolution around the Sun.
Q: What is the axial tilt of the Earth?
A: The Earth's axis is tilted at an angle of about 23.5 degrees from the vertical.
Q: What causes the seasons on Earth?
A: Seasons are caused by the Earth's axial tilt of 23.5 degrees and its revolution around the Sun, which changes the angle and duration of sunlight in different regions.
Q: Why does Earth have seasons and not just one climate?
A: Because the tilted axis causes different parts of Earth to receive varying amounts of sunlight at different times of the year.
Q: What is a leap year?
A: A leap year has 366 days and occurs every 4 years to account for the extra 0.25 day in Earth's revolution.
Q: When is the summer solstice in the Northern Hemisphere?
A: The summer solstice in the Northern Hemisphere occurs around June 21, when the North Pole is tilted towards the Sun.
Q: When is the winter solstice in the Northern Hemisphere?
A: The winter solstice in the Northern Hemisphere occurs around December 22, the shortest day of the year.
Q: What are the equinoxes?
A: Equinoxes are the two days a year (around March 21 and September 23) when day and night are of equal length worldwide.
Q: What is the vernal (spring) equinox?
A: The vernal equinox occurs around March 21 in the Northern Hemisphere, marking the beginning of spring.
Q: What is the autumnal equinox?
A: The autumnal equinox occurs around September 23 in the Northern Hemisphere, marking the beginning of autumn.
Q: What is the Earth's orbital plane called?
A: Earth's orbital plane is called the ecliptic plane.
Q: Why is the Sun directly overhead at the equator during equinoxes?
A: During equinoxes, the Sun's rays fall directly on the equator because the Earth's axis is neither tilted towards nor away from the Sun.
Q: What is the Circle of Illumination?
A: The Circle of Illumination is the imaginary line that divides the Earth into day and night hemispheres.
Q: In which direction does the Earth rotate?
A: The Earth rotates from west to east, which is why the Sun appears to rise in the east.
Q: What would happen if the Earth's axis were not tilted?
A: Without the axial tilt, there would be no seasons, and day length would be constant throughout the year.
Q: Why are days longer in summer and shorter in winter?
A: Because of the axial tilt, the Sun's path across the sky is longer in summer and shorter in winter in each hemisphere.
Q: What are the tropics related to Earth's tilt?
A: The Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N) and Tropic of Capricorn (23.5°S) are the latitudes where the Sun is directly overhead at the solstices, determined by the 23.5° tilt.
Q: What is the difference between rotation and revolution?
A: Rotation is Earth's spin on its own axis (causes day/night), while revolution is Earth's orbit around the Sun (causes seasons).
Q: What is the actual length of a solar day?
A: A solar day (noon to noon) is 24 hours long, while the sidereal day is about 23 hours 56 minutes.
Q: At which latitude does the Sun remain above the horizon for 24 hours on the summer solstice?
A: Within the Arctic Circle (66.5°N), the Sun remains above the horizon for 24 hours during the summer solstice, called the Midnight Sun.
Q: What is perihelion?
A: Perihelion is the point in Earth's orbit when it is closest to the Sun, occurring around January 3.
Q: What is aphelion?
A: Aphelion is the point in Earth's orbit when it is farthest from the Sun, occurring around July 4.

A: Yes. All questions, answers and explanations for Earth: Rotation, Revolution, Inclination & Seasons are completely free, with no login or payment required.

A: Yes. Every question and answer in this topic is bilingual, so you can practise in Assamese and English.

### Latitudes, Longitudes, Equator & International Date Line | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/astronomical-geography-sec/latitudes-longitudes-equator-idl/
Summary: Important questions on latitudes, longitudes, the equator and the International Date Line for competitive exams. Relevant for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other government exams.
Q: What are latitudes?
A: Latitudes are imaginary horizontal lines that run east-west on the Earth, measuring distance north or south of the Equator.
Q: What are longitudes?
A: Longitudes are imaginary vertical lines that run from the North Pole to the South Pole, measuring distance east or west of the Prime Meridian.
Q: What is the Equator?
A: The Equator is the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth, at 0 degrees latitude, dividing it into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
Q: What is the Prime Meridian?
A: The Prime Meridian is the line of 0 degrees longitude, passing through Greenwich, England, dividing Earth into Eastern and Western Hemispheres.
Q: What is the range of latitude values?
A: Latitude ranges from 0 degrees at the Equator to 90 degrees North at the North Pole and 90 degrees South at the South Pole.
Q: What is the range of longitude values?
A: Longitude ranges from 0 degrees at the Prime Meridian to 180 degrees east and 180 degrees west.
Q: What is the standard latitude of the Tropic of Cancer?
A: The Tropic of Cancer is located at 23.5 degrees North latitude.
Q: What is the standard latitude of the Tropic of Capricorn?
A: The Tropic of Capricorn is located at 23.5 degrees South latitude.
Q: What is the latitude of the Arctic Circle?
A: The Arctic Circle is located at 66.5 degrees North latitude.
Q: What is the latitude of the Antarctic Circle?
A: The Antarctic Circle is located at 66.5 degrees South latitude.
Q: What are the five important parallels of latitude?
A: The five important parallels are the Equator (0°), Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N), Tropic of Capricorn (23.5°S), Arctic Circle (66.5°N), and Antarctic Circle (66.5°S).
Q: What is the International Date Line?
A: The International Date Line is an imaginary line near 180 degrees longitude in the Pacific Ocean, where the date changes by one day when crossed.
Q: Where does the International Date Line deviate?
A: The International Date Line deviates around islands in the Pacific, such as Fiji, Tonga, and the Aleutian Islands, to keep them in the same day.
Q: What happens when you cross the International Date Line going west?
A: When crossing the International Date Line going west (from east to west), you gain a day (add one day).
Q: What happens when you cross the International Date Line going east?
A: When crossing the International Date Line going east, you lose a day (subtract one day).
Q: Why is the International Date Line not a straight line?
A: It is not straight because it is bent to avoid dividing island groups and political territories, keeping them on the same date.
Q: What is the relation between longitudes and time?
A: The Earth rotates 360 degrees in 24 hours, so each 15 degrees of longitude corresponds to one hour of time difference.
Q: How many degrees does the Earth rotate in one hour?
A: The Earth rotates 15 degrees in one hour (360 degrees divided by 24 hours).
Q: What is the Greenwich Meridian Time (GMT)?
A: GMT is the mean solar time at the Prime Meridian (0 degrees longitude) at Greenwich, England, used as a time reference.
Q: Which city is located near the Prime Meridian?
A: Greenwich in London, England is located near the Prime Meridian.
Q: What is the difference between latitudes and longitudes in terms of lines?
A: Latitudes are parallel horizontal lines of equal spacing, while longitudes are vertical lines that converge at the poles.
Q: How many longitudes are there in total?
A: There are 360 longitudes in total (180 east and 180 west, including the 0 and 180 degree lines).
Q: How many latitudes are there?
A: There are 181 latitudes including the Equator (90 north, 90 south, and the Equator), if counted by whole degrees.
Q: Which country does the Equator pass through in South America?
A: The Equator passes through Ecuador, Colombia, and Brazil in South America.
Q: What is the length of the equator?
A: The circumference of the Earth at the Equator is about 40,075 kilometers.

A: Yes. All questions, answers and explanations for Latitudes, Longitudes, Equator & International Date Line are completely free, with no login or payment required.

A: Yes. Every question and answer in this topic is bilingual, so you can practise in Assamese and English.

### Moon: Phases, Solar & Lunar Eclipses | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/astronomical-geography-sec/moon-phases-eclipses-tides/
Summary: Important questions on the Moon's phases, solar eclipses and lunar eclipses for competitive exams. Practice for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What is the Moon?
A: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite, a rocky body that orbits Earth about once every 27.3 days.
Q: What are the phases of the Moon?
A: The main phases are New Moon, Waxing Crescent, First Quarter, Waxing Gibbous, Full Moon, Waning Gibbous, Last Quarter, and Waning Crescent.
Q: What causes the phases of the Moon?
A: The phases are caused by the changing angle of sunlight illuminating the Moon as it orbits the Earth, showing different portions of its lit half.
Q: What is a New Moon?
A: A New Moon occurs when the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, so its illuminated side faces away from Earth and it appears dark.
Q: What is a Full Moon?
A: A Full Moon occurs when the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, so the entire illuminated side of the Moon faces Earth.
Q: What is a lunar month or synodic month?
A: A synodic month is the time between two successive new moons, about 29.5 days.
Q: What is a sidereal month?
A: A sidereal month is the time the Moon takes to orbit Earth relative to the stars, about 27.3 days.
Q: What is a solar eclipse?
A: A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, blocking the Sun's light.
Q: When does a solar eclipse occur?
A: A solar eclipse occurs during a New Moon, when the Moon is aligned between the Sun and Earth.
Q: What is a lunar eclipse?
A: A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, casting Earth's shadow on the Moon.
Q: When does a lunar eclipse occur?
A: A lunar eclipse occurs during a Full Moon, when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in a straight line with Earth in the middle.
Q: What is a total solar eclipse?
A: A total solar eclipse occurs when the Moon completely covers the Sun, visible from a narrow path on Earth, and the corona becomes visible.
Q: What is a partial solar eclipse?
A: A partial solar eclipse occurs when only a part of the Sun is covered by the Moon.
Q: What is an annular solar eclipse?
A: An annular solar eclipse occurs when the Moon is farther from Earth and does not fully cover the Sun, leaving a bright ring (annulus) around it.
Q: What is the difference between a total and partial lunar eclipse?
A: In a total lunar eclipse, the Moon fully enters Earth's umbra and turns red; in a partial lunar eclipse, only part of the Moon enters the umbra.
Q: What is the umbra and penumbra?
A: The umbra is the darkest, central part of a shadow where light is fully blocked, while the penumbra is the lighter outer part where light is partially blocked.
Q: Why does the Moon appear red during a total lunar eclipse?
A: During a total lunar eclipse, Earth's atmosphere bends red light into the shadow, so the Moon appears reddish, called the Blood Moon.
Q: How often do eclipses occur?
A: Solar and lunar eclipses occur in pairs about two weeks apart, roughly 4 to 7 times a year in some combination.
Q: Why do we not have eclipses every month?
A: Eclipses do not occur every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit, so the Moon usually passes above or below the shadow.
Q: What is the Saros cycle?
A: The Saros cycle is a period of about 18 years and 11 days after which similar eclipses repeat.
Q: Which is more visible: solar or lunar eclipse?
A: A lunar eclipse is visible from the entire night-side hemisphere of Earth, while a solar eclipse is visible only from a narrow path.
Q: Why is looking at a solar eclipse directly dangerous?
A: Directly looking at a solar eclipse can damage the retina permanently, so special eclipse glasses are needed.
Q: What is the Moon's orbit direction around Earth?
A: The Moon orbits Earth in a counterclockwise direction (when viewed from above the North Pole), same as Earth's rotation.
Q: What is the Moon's average distance from Earth?
A: The Moon's average distance from Earth is about 384,400 kilometers.
Q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
A: We always see the same side because the Moon's rotation period matches its orbital period, a state called tidal locking.

### Nebulae, Black Holes & Supernovae | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/astronomical-geography-sec/nebulae-blackholes-supernovae/
Summary: Important questions on nebulae, black holes and supernovae for competitive exams. Covers ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What is a nebula?
A: A nebula is a giant cloud of gas and dust in space, often a birthplace of stars.
Q: What are the main types of nebulae?
A: The main types are emission nebulae, reflection nebulae, dark nebulae, and planetary nebulae.
Q: What is an emission nebula?
A: An emission nebula is a cloud of ionized gas that emits light of various colors, often red due to hydrogen.
Q: What is a planetary nebula?
A: A planetary nebula is a glowing shell of gas ejected by a Sun-like star near the end of its life, not related to planets.
Q: What is a supernova?
A: A supernova is a powerful and bright explosion of a star at the end of its life, briefly outshining an entire galaxy.
Q: What are the two main types of supernovae?
A: The two main types are Type I (white dwarf explosion) and Type II (core-collapse of a massive star).
Q: What is left after a supernova of a massive star?
A: After a supernova, the core can become a neutron star or a black hole, surrounded by a supernova remnant.
Q: What is the Crab Nebula?
A: The Crab Nebula is a supernova remnant in the constellation Taurus, created by a supernova observed in 1054 AD.
Q: What is a black hole?
A: A black hole is a region in space with such strong gravity that nothing, not even light, can escape from it.
Q: What is the event horizon of a black hole?
A: The event horizon is the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing, including light, can escape.
Q: What is a singularity?
A: A singularity is a point of infinite density at the center of a black hole where the known laws of physics break down.
Q: Who proposed the theory of black holes based on general relativity?
A: Albert Einstein's general relativity predicted black holes, and Karl Schwarzschild provided the first solution.
Q: What is a supermassive black hole?
A: A supermassive black hole has millions to billions of times the Sun's mass and is found at the center of most galaxies.
Q: What is the first black hole ever photographed?
A: The first black hole photographed is the supermassive black hole M87* in the Messier 87 galaxy, imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2019.
Q: What is Hawking radiation?
A: Hawking radiation is the theoretical radiation that black holes emit due to quantum effects near the event horizon, causing them to slowly lose mass.
Q: Who proposed Hawking radiation?
A: Stephen Hawking proposed Hawking radiation in 1974.
Q: What is the Chandrasekhar limit?
A: The Chandrasekhar limit is about 1.4 times the Sun's mass; beyond this, a white dwarf collapses into a neutron star or black hole. It was calculated by Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar.
Q: What is the Great Red Spot related to nebulae or stars?
A: No, the Great Red Spot is a giant storm on Jupiter, not a nebula or star.
Q: What is a dark nebula?
A: A dark nebula is a dense cloud of dust that blocks the light of stars behind it, appearing as a dark patch in the sky.
Q: What is the Horsehead Nebula?
A: The Horsehead Nebula is a famous dark nebula in the constellation Orion, shaped like a horse's head.
Q: What is a stellar black hole?
A: A stellar black hole is formed when a massive star (about 20 times the Sun's mass) collapses after a supernova.
Q: What is spaghettification?
A: Spaghettification is the stretching of an object into a long thin shape due to extreme tidal forces near a black hole.
Q: What element is produced in supernova explosions?
A: Supernovae produce heavy elements like iron, gold, silver, and uranium through rapid nuclear processes.
Q: What is an accretion disk?
A: An accretion disk is a rotating disk of gas and dust that spirals into a black hole or young star, heated to very high temperatures.
Q: What is the Pillars of Creation?
A: The Pillars of Creation is a famous structure of interstellar gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula, where new stars are forming.

### Planetary Moons: Titan, Ganymede & Europa | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/astronomical-geography-sec/planetary-moons-titan-ganymede-europa/
Summary: Important questions on planetary moons such as Titan, Ganymede and Europa for competitive exams. Covers ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What is a natural satellite?
A: A natural satellite, or moon, is a celestial body that orbits a planet. Earth's natural satellite is the Moon.
Q: What is Titan?
A: Titan is the largest moon of Saturn and the second-largest moon in the solar system.
Q: What is Titan's atmosphere made of?
A: Titan has a thick atmosphere made mostly of nitrogen, with methane and other hydrocarbons.
Q: What is unique about the surface of Titan?
A: Titan is the only moon with a dense atmosphere and has lakes and rivers of liquid methane and ethane on its surface.
Q: Which moon is the largest in the solar system?
A: Ganymede, a moon of Jupiter, is the largest moon in the solar system.
Q: What is special about Ganymede?
A: Ganymede is the largest moon, is larger than the planet Mercury, and is the only moon known to have its own magnetic field.
Q: What is Europa?
A: Europa is a moon of Jupiter, known for its smooth icy surface and suspected subsurface ocean.
Q: Why is Europa considered a candidate for life?
A: Europa is considered a candidate for life because it likely has a subsurface ocean of liquid water beneath its icy crust.
Q: How many moons does Jupiter have?
A: Jupiter has over 90 confirmed moons, with the four largest being the Galilean moons.
Q: Who discovered the four largest moons of Jupiter?
A: Galileo Galilei discovered the four largest moons of Jupiter in 1610.
Q: What are the four Galilean moons?
A: The four Galilean moons are Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto.
Q: Which moon has active volcanoes?
A: Io, a moon of Jupiter, is the most volcanically active body in the solar system.
Q: How many moons does Saturn have?
A: Saturn has over 140 confirmed moons, making it the planet with the most known moons.
Q: Which moon of Saturn has geysers of water?
A: Enceladus, a moon of Saturn, has geysers of water ice erupting from its south pole, suggesting a subsurface ocean.
Q: Which moon has a retrograde orbit around Neptune?
A: Triton, the largest moon of Neptune, has a retrograde orbit, meaning it orbits opposite to Neptune's rotation.
Q: What is Earth's Moon's diameter?
A: The Moon's diameter is about 3,474 kilometers, about one-fourth the diameter of Earth.
Q: Which moon is known as a 'water world' candidate?
A: Europa is the main 'water world' candidate, with a vast ocean of liquid water beneath its icy crust.
Q: What is the atmosphere like on Ganymede?
A: Ganymede has a very thin atmosphere of oxygen and ozone.
Q: What mission studied Titan up close?
A: NASA's Cassini mission, with the Huygens probe that landed on Titan in 2005, studied Titan closely.
Q: What is the 'Dragonfly' mission?
A: Dragonfly is a NASA mission to send a rotorcraft drone to explore the surface of Titan.
Q: What is the largest moon of Uranus?
A: Titania is the largest moon of Uranus.
Q: Which moon is the brightest object in the sky after the Sun?
A: Earth's Moon is the brightest object in the night sky after the Sun.
Q: What causes the moons' phases from Earth?
A: The Moon's phases are caused by the changing angle of sunlight illuminating the Moon as it orbits Earth.
Q: What is Callisto?
A: Callisto is the second-largest Galilean moon of Jupiter, known for its heavily cratered ancient surface.
Q: What is a Trojan moon or satellite system?
A: A Trojan moon is a small moon that orbits a planet in the same orbit as a larger moon, at a stable Lagrange point.

### Inner & Outer Planets: Order, Sizes & Facts | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/astronomical-geography-sec/solar-system-planets-order-sizes/
Summary: Important questions on the order, sizes and facts of the inner and outer planets for competitive exams. Practice for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: How many planets are there in our solar system?
A: There are 8 planets in our solar system.
Q: What is the correct order of planets from the Sun?
A: The order is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.
Q: What are the inner (terrestrial) planets?
A: The inner planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. They are small, rocky planets.
Q: What are the outer (gas giant) planets?
A: The outer planets are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. They are large and mostly made of gas and ice.
Q: Which is the largest planet in the solar system?
A: Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system.
Q: Which is the smallest planet in the solar system?
A: Mercury is the smallest planet in the solar system.
Q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
A: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun.
Q: Which planet is the hottest in the solar system?
A: Venus is the hottest planet due to its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere causing a runaway greenhouse effect.
Q: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
A: Mars is known as the Red Planet because of the iron oxide (rust) on its surface.
Q: Which planet is known as Earth's twin?
A: Venus is known as Earth's twin because of its similar size and mass.
Q: Which planet has the most moons?
A: Saturn has the most confirmed moons (over 140 as of recent counts), though Jupiter also has many (over 90).
Q: Which planet is famous for its ring system?
A: Saturn is most famous for its spectacular ring system made of ice and rock particles.
Q: Which planet rotates on its side?
A: Uranus rotates on its side, with an axial tilt of about 98 degrees.
Q: Which planet has the strongest winds?
A: Neptune has the strongest winds in the solar system, reaching up to 2,100 km/h.
Q: Which planet is known as the Blue Planet?
A: Earth is known as the Blue Planet because of its abundant water, and Neptune is also blue due to methane in its atmosphere.
Q: Which is the only planet with life?
A: Earth is the only known planet that supports life.
Q: What is the Great Red Spot?
A: The Great Red Spot is a giant, persistent storm on Jupiter, larger than Earth.
Q: Which planet is called the Morning Star and Evening Star?
A: Venus is called the Morning Star and Evening Star because it is visible in the east before sunrise and in the west after sunset.
Q: Which planet has a day longer than its year?
A: Venus has a day (243 Earth days) longer than its year (225 Earth days).
Q: Which planet spins in the opposite direction?
A: Venus and Uranus spin in the opposite (retrograde) direction compared to most planets.
Q: What is the asteroid belt?
A: The asteroid belt is a region of rocky objects between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
Q: Which planet is the densest in the solar system?
A: Earth is the densest planet in the solar system.
Q: Which planet has the largest volcano?
A: Mars has the largest volcano, Olympus Mons, which is about 22 km high.
Q: Which planet has no moons?
A: Mercury and Venus have no moons.
Q: Which planet is farthest from the Sun?
A: Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun.

### Indian Missions: Chandrayaan, Mangalyaan & Aditya-L1 | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/astronomical-geography-sec/space-agencies-missions-isro-nasa/
Summary: Important questions on Indian space missions including Chandrayaan, Mangalyaan and Aditya-L1 for competitive exams. Covers ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What is ISRO?
A: ISRO stands for Indian Space Research Organisation, India's national space agency headquartered in Bengaluru.
Q: When was ISRO founded?
A: ISRO was founded in 1969, with Vikram Sarabhai as its founding chairman.
Q: What is Chandrayaan?
A: Chandrayaan is ISRO's series of lunar missions, meaning 'Moon craft' in Sanskrit, aimed at exploring the Moon.
Q: When was Chandrayaan-1 launched?
A: Chandrayaan-1 was launched on October 22, 2008, using the PSLV-C11 rocket.
Q: What was the major discovery of Chandrayaan-1?
A: Chandrayaan-1 discovered water molecules on the Moon's surface using its Moon Impact Probe and NASA's M3 instrument.
Q: When was Chandrayaan-2 launched?
A: Chandrayaan-2 was launched on July 22, 2019, using the GSLV Mk III-M1 rocket.
Q: What were the components of Chandrayaan-2?
A: Chandrayaan-2 consisted of an orbiter, a lander called Vikram, and a rover called Pragyan.
Q: What happened to the Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-2?
A: The Vikram lander lost contact during its final descent and hard-landed on the Moon on September 6, 2019.
Q: When was Chandrayaan-3 launched?
A: Chandrayaan-3 was launched on July 14, 2023, using the LVM3-M4 rocket.
Q: When did Chandrayaan-3's Vikram lander land on the Moon?
A: The Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-3 successfully soft-landed near the lunar south pole on August 23, 2023.
Q: Which country became the first to land near the lunar south pole?
A: India became the first country to land near the lunar south pole with Chandrayaan-3.
Q: What was the name of the Chandrayaan-3 rover?
A: The Chandrayaan-3 rover was called Pragyan, and the lander was called Vikram.
Q: What did Chandrayaan-3's Pragyan rover find on the Moon?
A: The Pragyan rover found sulphur, iron, and other elements near the lunar south pole, and confirmed the presence of water ice.
Q: What is Mangalyaan?
A: Mangalyaan, or the Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM), is ISRO's Mars mission, meaning 'Mars craft' in Sanskrit.
Q: When was Mangalyaan launched?
A: Mangalyaan was launched on November 5, 2013, using the PSLV-C25 rocket.
Q: When did Mangalyaan enter Mars orbit?
A: Mangalyaan entered Mars orbit on September 24, 2014, on its first attempt.
Q: What was unique about Mangalyaan?
A: Mangalyaan made India the first country to reach Mars orbit on its first attempt, and the cheapest Mars mission at that time.
Q: Which country reached Mars on the first attempt before India?
A: No country reached Mars on the first attempt before India; India was the first to do so.
Q: What is Aditya-L1?
A: Aditya-L1 is ISRO's first solar observatory mission, aimed at studying the Sun from the L1 Lagrange point.
Q: When was Aditya-L1 launched?
A: Aditya-L1 was launched on September 2, 2023, using the PSLV-C57 rocket.
Q: What is the L1 Lagrange point?
A: The L1 point is a location about 1.5 million km from Earth towards the Sun, where gravitational forces balance, allowing continuous observation of the Sun.
Q: What does Aditya-L1 study?
A: Aditya-L1 studies the solar corona, solar wind, solar flares, and space weather using seven payloads.
Q: When did Aditya-L1 reach the L1 point?
A: Aditya-L1 reached the L1 point on January 6, 2024, and was placed in a halo orbit.
Q: Which rocket was used for Chandrayaan-1?
A: Chandrayaan-1 was launched using the PSLV-C11 rocket.
Q: What is the significance of the landing site of Chandrayaan-3?
A: The lunar south pole region is significant because it contains permanently shadowed craters with water ice, which could support future missions and habitation.

### Stars: Lifecycle, Constellations & Light Year | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/astronomical-geography-sec/stars-lifecycle-constellations-lightyear/
Summary: Important questions on the lifecycle of stars, constellations and the light year for competitive exams. Relevant for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other government exams.
Q: What is a star?
A: A star is a massive, luminous ball of hot plasma (gas) that produces energy through nuclear fusion in its core.
Q: What is the first stage in the lifecycle of a star?
A: A star begins as a nebula (cloud of gas and dust), which contracts to form a protostar.
Q: What is a protostar?
A: A protostar is a young star still gathering mass from its surrounding cloud before nuclear fusion begins in its core.
Q: What is the main sequence stage of a star?
A: The main sequence is the longest and most stable stage when a star fuses hydrogen into helium in its core, like our Sun.
Q: What happens when a star exhausts its hydrogen fuel?
A: The star expands into a red giant (for medium stars) or red supergiant (for massive stars) and begins fusing heavier elements.
Q: What is a red giant?
A: A red giant is a large, cool, and luminous star that forms near the end of a Sun-like star's life when its core contracts and outer layers expand.
Q: What is the final stage of a Sun-like star?
A: A Sun-like star ends as a white dwarf, surrounded by a planetary nebula.
Q: What is a white dwarf?
A: A white dwarf is the dense, hot remnant core of a star that has exhausted its nuclear fuel and shed its outer layers.
Q: What is a neutron star?
A: A neutron star is an extremely dense remnant left after a supernova explosion of a massive star, composed mainly of neutrons.
Q: What is a pulsar?
A: A pulsar is a rapidly rotating neutron star that emits beams of radiation, which appear as regular pulses when observed from Earth.
Q: What determines the final fate of a star?
A: The mass of the star is the main factor that determines its final fate - white dwarf, neutron star, or black hole.
Q: What is a constellation?
A: A constellation is a recognizable pattern or group of stars in the sky that has been given a name, like Orion or the Big Dipper.
Q: How many constellations are officially recognized?
A: The International Astronomical Union (IAU) officially recognizes 88 constellations.
Q: What is a light year?
A: A light year is the distance that light travels in one year, equal to about 9.46 trillion kilometers.
Q: What is the distance of one light year in kilometers?
A: One light year is approximately 9.46 trillion kilometers (about 9.461 × 10^12 km).
Q: What is the speed of light?
A: The speed of light in a vacuum is approximately 300,000 kilometers per second (3 × 10^8 m/s).
Q: Which is the brightest star in the night sky?
A: Sirius (Dog Star) is the brightest star in the night sky, located in the constellation Canis Major.
Q: Which star is nearest to the Sun?
A: Proxima Centauri is the nearest star to the Sun, located about 4.24 light-years away.
Q: What is the color of the hottest stars?
A: The hottest stars appear blue or blue-white in color, while cooler stars appear red.
Q: What is a binary star system?
A: A binary star system is a pair of stars that orbit around their common center of mass.
Q: What is nuclear fusion in stars?
A: Nuclear fusion is the process in which hydrogen atoms combine to form helium, releasing enormous amounts of energy.
Q: What is a shooting star?
A: A shooting star is actually a meteor - a small piece of rock or dust burning up in Earth's atmosphere, not a real star.
Q: What is the Hertzsprung-Russell (H-R) diagram?
A: The H-R diagram plots stars based on their luminosity and temperature, showing the stages of stellar evolution.
Q: Which constellation contains the North Star (Polaris)?
A: Polaris, the North Star, is located in the constellation Ursa Minor (Little Dipper), at the tip of its tail.
Q: What is a brown dwarf?
A: A brown dwarf is an object too massive to be a planet but too small to sustain nuclear fusion, so it shines faintly in infrared.

### Sun: Structure, Core & Solar Flares | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/astronomical-geography-sec/sun-structure-core-flares/
Summary: Important questions on the Sun's structure, core and solar flares for competitive exams. Covers ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What is the Sun?
A: The Sun is a star, a giant ball of hot plasma, at the center of our solar system. It is a G-type main-sequence star (yellow dwarf).
Q: What is the Sun mainly made of?
A: The Sun is mainly composed of hydrogen (about 74%) and helium (about 24%), with small amounts of other elements.
Q: What are the layers of the Sun's interior?
A: The interior layers of the Sun are the core, radiative zone, and convective zone.
Q: What are the layers of the Sun's atmosphere?
A: The Sun's atmosphere consists of the photosphere, chromosphere, and corona.
Q: What is the temperature of the Sun's core?
A: The temperature of the Sun's core is about 15 million degrees Celsius (27 million degrees Fahrenheit).
Q: What process produces the Sun's energy?
A: The Sun produces energy through nuclear fusion, in which hydrogen atoms fuse into helium in the core.
Q: What is the proton-proton chain?
A: The proton-proton chain is the series of nuclear fusion reactions in the Sun's core that convert hydrogen into helium, releasing energy.
Q: What is the photosphere?
A: The photosphere is the visible surface of the Sun, with a temperature of about 5,500 degrees Celsius, from which sunlight is emitted.
Q: What is the corona?
A: The corona is the outermost, very hot layer of the Sun's atmosphere, visible during a total solar eclipse.
Q: What is the temperature of the corona?
A: The corona is surprisingly much hotter than the surface, with temperatures of 1 to 3 million degrees Celsius.
Q: What are sunspots?
A: Sunspots are darker, cooler areas on the Sun's surface caused by strong magnetic activity.
Q: What is a solar flare?
A: A solar flare is a sudden, intense burst of radiation from the Sun's surface, caused by the release of magnetic energy.
Q: What is a coronal mass ejection (CME)?
A: A coronal mass ejection is a massive burst of plasma and magnetic field ejected from the Sun's corona into space.
Q: What is the solar wind?
A: The solar wind is a continuous stream of charged particles (plasma) flowing outward from the Sun's corona.
Q: What are auroras caused by?
A: Auroras are caused by charged solar particles interacting with Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere near the poles.
Q: What is the Sun's rotation period?
A: The Sun rotates at different speeds at different latitudes; about 25 days at the equator and about 35 days at the poles.
Q: What is the Sun's average distance from Earth?
A: The Sun's average distance from Earth is about 149.6 million kilometers, called one astronomical unit (AU).
Q: How long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
A: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth.
Q: What is the Sun's mass compared to the solar system?
A: The Sun contains about 99.86% of the total mass of the entire solar system.
Q: What is the Sun's lifecycle stage?
A: The Sun is currently in the main sequence stage, about halfway through its 10 billion year life.
Q: What will the Sun become in about 5 billion years?
A: The Sun will expand into a red giant and then end as a white dwarf surrounded by a planetary nebula.
Q: What is the solar cycle?
A: The solar cycle is the roughly 11-year cycle of sunspot and solar activity on the Sun.
Q: What is the solar constant?
A: The solar constant is the amount of solar energy received per unit area at the top of Earth's atmosphere, about 1,361 watts per square meter.
Q: What is the age of the Sun?
A: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old.
Q: Which mission studies the Sun?
A: India's Aditya-L1 mission and NASA's Parker Solar Probe are missions that study the Sun.

### Time Zones & Standard Time Calculation | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/astronomical-geography-sec/timezones-standard-time-calculation/
Summary: Important questions on time zones and standard time calculation for competitive exams. Practice for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What is a time zone?
A: A time zone is a region of the Earth where the same standard time is used, generally based on 15 degrees of longitude intervals.
Q: How many time zones exist around the world?
A: Ideally there are 24 time zones (360 degrees divided by 15 degrees), but in practice there are about 40, counting irregular ones.
Q: What is the standard meridian of India?
A: India's standard meridian is 82.5 degrees East, which passes through Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh.
Q: What is Indian Standard Time (IST)?
A: Indian Standard Time is UTC+5:30, the time used uniformly across India.
Q: What is UTC?
A: UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) is the primary global time standard, roughly equivalent to GMT, used as a reference for all time zones.
Q: Why is India's standard meridian 82.5°E?
A: The 82.5°E meridian was chosen so that a single time zone covers the whole country uniformly, avoiding multiple time zones.
Q: How do you calculate time difference between two places based on longitude?
A: Divide the difference in longitude by 15 to get the time difference in hours; each 15 degrees equals 1 hour.
Q: If it is 12 noon at Greenwich (0°), what is the local time at 15°E?
A: At 15°E, the local time is 1:00 PM, because it is east and ahead of Greenwich.
Q: How is time calculated for a place east of the Prime Meridian?
A: For places east of the Prime Meridian, add the time difference to the GMT/UTC to get local time.
Q: How is time calculated for a place west of the Prime Meridian?
A: For places west of the Prime Meridian, subtract the time difference from the GMT/UTC to get local time.
Q: What is the formula to find longitude from time difference?
A: Multiply the time difference in hours by 15 degrees to get the longitude difference (Time difference × 15° = Longitude difference).
Q: What is daylight saving time (DST)?
A: Daylight Saving Time is the practice of advancing clocks by one hour during summer months to extend evening daylight.
Q: Does India observe daylight saving time?
A: No, India does not observe daylight saving time; it uses IST (UTC+5:30) all year round.
Q: What is Greenwich Mean Time (GMT)?
A: GMT is the mean solar time at the Prime Meridian (0° longitude) at Greenwich, London, used as the historical global time reference.
Q: What is the difference between GMT and UTC?
A: GMT is based on the Earth's rotation and is an astronomical time, while UTC is an atomic time standard with occasional leap seconds.
Q: Which country spans the most time zones?
A: France spans the most time zones (about 12), including its overseas territories; Russia spans 11 time zones.
Q: What is the standard time of the USA (EST)?
A: Eastern Standard Time (EST) of the USA is UTC-5, and Eastern Daylight Time is UTC-4.
Q: What is the time in India when it is 12 noon GMT?
A: When it is 12 noon GMT, it is 5:30 PM in India (IST = GMT + 5:30).
Q: What is a local mean time?
A: Local mean time is the average solar time at a specific longitude, based on the position of the Sun at that meridian.
Q: Which line of longitude is used for the International Date Line's basis?
A: The International Date Line is based on the 180 degrees longitude line.
Q: What happens to the date when crossing the International Date Line from east to west?
A: Crossing the International Date Line from east to west, you add one day (move forward in date).
Q: If a place is at 45°E and Greenwich is at 0°, what is the local time when it is 12 noon at Greenwich?
A: The time difference is 45/15 = 3 hours. Since the place is east, local time is 3:00 PM.
Q: What is China's standard time?
A: China uses a single standard time zone, Beijing Time, which is UTC+8.
Q: Why does Japan use UTC+9?
A: Japan Standard Time is UTC+9, determined by the 135°E meridian, which is 9 hours ahead of GMT.
Q: What is the problem with the International Date Line in terms of time zones?
A: The problem is that adjacent places on either side of the line can have dates that differ by one day, even if they are close in location.

### Big Bang Theory & Galaxies | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/astronomical-geography-sec/universe-bigbang-galaxies/
Summary: Important questions on the Big Bang theory and galaxies for competitive exams. Covers ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What is the Big Bang Theory?
A: The Big Bang Theory states that the universe began from a single, extremely hot and dense point about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since.
Q: Who proposed the Big Bang Theory?
A: The term 'Big Bang' was coined by Fred Hoyle, but the theory was developed by Georges Lemaitre, who proposed that the universe began from a primeval atom.
Q: What evidence supports the Big Bang Theory?
A: The main evidence includes cosmic microwave background radiation, the redshift of distant galaxies (Hubble's law), and the abundance of light elements like hydrogen and helium.
Q: What is cosmic microwave background radiation (CMB)?
A: CMB is the faint thermal radiation left over from the Big Bang, filling the universe. It was discovered by Penzias and Wilson in 1965.
Q: What is a galaxy?
A: A galaxy is a huge system of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter bound together by gravity. Our galaxy is the Milky Way.
Q: What type of galaxy is the Milky Way?
A: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy with a central bar-shaped structure and spiral arms.
Q: How many galaxies are estimated to exist in the observable universe?
A: It is estimated that there are more than 100 billion to 200 billion galaxies in the observable universe.
Q: What are the three main types of galaxies?
A: The three main types of galaxies are spiral, elliptical, and irregular galaxies.
Q: What is Hubble's Law?
A: Hubble's Law states that the velocity at which a galaxy recedes from us is directly proportional to its distance, showing that the universe is expanding.
Q: Who discovered that galaxies are moving away from us?
A: Edwin Hubble discovered in 1929 that galaxies are moving away from us, based on their redshift.
Q: What is dark matter?
A: Dark matter is an invisible form of matter that does not emit or absorb light but exerts gravitational effects. It makes up about 27% of the universe.
Q: What is dark energy?
A: Dark energy is a mysterious force that is causing the accelerated expansion of the universe. It makes up about 68% of the universe.
Q: What is the Local Group?
A: The Local Group is a cluster of about 80 galaxies that includes the Milky Way, Andromeda, and the Magellanic Clouds.
Q: What is the nearest large galaxy to the Milky Way?
A: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) is the nearest large spiral galaxy to the Milky Way, located about 2.5 million light-years away.
Q: What is a quasar?
A: A quasar is an extremely bright, distant galactic nucleus powered by a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy.
Q: What is a supernova remnant related to?
A: A supernova remnant is the expanding debris cloud left behind after a supernova explosion of a star.
Q: What is the 'Big Bang' age of the universe?
A: The universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old according to the Big Bang Theory.
Q: What was the state of the universe before the Big Bang?
A: The universe existed as a singular, infinitely hot and dense point called a singularity, with no space or time.
Q: What element was formed first after the Big Bang?
A: Hydrogen and helium were the first elements formed after the Big Bang, with hydrogen being the most abundant.
Q: What is a black hole's connection to galaxies?
A: Most large galaxies are believed to have a supermassive black hole at their center, which affects the galaxy's evolution and motion of stars.
Q: What is redshift?
A: Redshift is the increase in wavelength of light from a distant object moving away from us, indicating the object is receding.
Q: What is the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole called?
A: The supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way is called Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*).
Q: Which satellite galaxy of the Milky Way is visible from the southern hemisphere?
A: The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are satellite galaxies of the Milky Way visible from the southern hemisphere.
Q: What is the Great Attractor?
A: The Great Attractor is a massive gravitational anomaly in space toward which our galaxy and many others are moving.
Q: What does the expansion of the universe mean for galaxy distances?
A: It means that on average, the distances between galaxies are increasing over time, so distant galaxies are moving farther apart.

### Upcoming Missions: Gaganyaan & Shukrayaan | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/astronomical-geography-sec/upcoming-missions-space-telescopes/
Summary: Important questions on upcoming Indian space missions such as Gaganyaan and Shukrayaan for competitive exams. Relevant for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other government exams.
Q: What is the Gaganyaan mission?
A: Gaganyaan is ISRO's first crewed spaceflight mission, which will send Indian astronauts to low Earth orbit and bring them back safely.
Q: What does the name 'Gaganyaan' mean?
A: 'Gaganyaan' means 'Sky craft' in Sanskrit, referring to a space vehicle.
Q: Which agency is responsible for Gaganyaan?
A: ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation) is responsible for the Gaganyaan mission, with support from HAL and DRDO.
Q: How many astronauts will Gaganyaan carry?
A: The Gaganyaan mission is planned to carry up to 3 astronauts (vyomanauts) into orbit.
Q: What is the planned duration of the Gaganyaan crewed mission?
A: The Gaganyaan crewed mission is planned to last up to 3 days in low Earth orbit.
Q: Which rocket will launch the Gaganyaan mission?
A: The Gaganyaan mission will be launched using the LVM3 (formerly GSLV Mk III) rocket.
Q: What is the crew module of Gaganyaan?
A: The crew module is the pressurized, habitable capsule that will carry the astronauts during the Gaganyaan mission.
Q: What is the Gaganyaan escape system?
A: The Crew Escape System (CES) is a safety mechanism that can pull the crew module away from the rocket in case of an emergency during launch.
Q: What was the first uncrewed test for Gaganyaan?
A: The first test was the pad abort test, called the TV-D1 flight, conducted on October 21, 2023, to test the crew escape system.
Q: What is the Vyomanaut Training Facility?
A: The Vyomanaut Training Facility is the facility in Bengaluru where the selected Indian astronauts are trained for the Gaganyaan mission.
Q: Which space agency collaborated with ISRO for Gaganyaan astronaut training?
A: Russia's Roscosmos initially collaborated with ISRO for the training of the Gaganyaan astronauts.
Q: What is the Chandrayaan-4 mission?
A: Chandrayaan-4 is a planned ISRO mission to collect lunar samples and return them to Earth, a sample-return mission.
Q: What is the LUPEX mission?
A: LUPEX (Lunar Polar Exploration) is a joint ISRO-JAXA mission to explore the lunar south pole region for water ice.
Q: What is the Shukrayaan mission?
A: Shukrayaan is ISRO's planned orbiter mission to Venus, aimed at studying the planet's atmosphere, surface, and environment.
Q: What does the name 'Shukrayaan' mean?
A: 'Shukrayaan' means 'Venus craft' in Sanskrit, as Shukra means Venus in Hindi/Sanskrit.
Q: Which countries have previously sent missions to Venus?
A: The USSR (Venera program), USA (Mariner, Magellan, Parker Solar Probe flyby), Japan (Akatsuki), and ESA (Venus Express) have sent missions to Venus.
Q: When was Shukrayaan expected to be launched?
A: Shukrayaan was earlier expected to launch around 2025-2026, but the schedule may be revised depending on ISRO's priorities.
Q: What will Shukrayaan study on Venus?
A: Shukrayaan will study Venus's atmosphere, surface features, volcanic activity, and investigate the planet's thick atmosphere and clouds.
Q: What is the Gaganyaan test vehicle (TV-D1)?
A: TV-D1 is the test vehicle used for the first pad abort test of Gaganyaan's crew escape system in October 2023.
Q: What is the purpose of the Gaganyaan G1/G2 uncrewed flights?
A: The G1 and G2 uncrewed flights will test the crew module, re-entry, and recovery systems before the final crewed mission.
Q: What is the planned Gaganyaan orbital altitude?
A: The Gaganyaan crewed mission is planned to operate in low Earth orbit at an altitude of about 400 kilometers.
Q: Which ISRO facility is the launch site for Gaganyaan?
A: Gaganyaan will be launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC) at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh.
Q: What is the Gaganyaan crew name in India?
A: Indian astronauts of the Gaganyaan mission are called 'Vyomanauts' (from Sanskrit 'Vyoma' meaning space).
Q: What is ISRO's NISAR mission?
A: NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) is a joint Earth-observation satellite mission to monitor changes in land, ice, and ecosystems.
Q: What is the future plan of ISRO regarding the Moon station?
A: ISRO plans to collaborate with JAXA and NASA in international lunar exploration, including the Lunar Gateway project and future sustained lunar presence.

### Climate, Monsoon and Soil Types | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/indian-geography-sec/climate-monsoon-soils-india/
Summary: Important questions on the climate, monsoon and soil types of India for Assam competitive exams. Relevant for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other government exams.
Q: What type of climate does India have?
A: Tropical monsoon type.
Q: What is the main reason for the monsoon in India?
A: The differential heating of land and sea and the shifting of the ITCZ.
Q: Which winds bring the southwest monsoon to India?
A: The moist southwest winds from the Indian Ocean.
Q: When does the southwest monsoon generally arrive in Kerala?
A: Around 1 June.
Q: When does the southwest monsoon arrive in Assam?
A: Around the first week of June.
Q: Which place of India receives the highest rainfall?
A: Mawsynram in Meghalaya.
Q: What is the average annual rainfall of Mawsynram?
A: About 11,000 millimetres.
Q: Which place of India receives the lowest rainfall?
A: Jaisalmer in Rajasthan (and Leh).
Q: What is the average annual rainfall of Assam?
A: About 2,000 to 3,000 millimetres.
Q: Which state of India receives the highest rainfall?
A: Meghalaya.
Q: What is the 'El Nino'?
A: The warming of the eastern Pacific Ocean waters that weakens the Indian monsoon.
Q: What is the 'La Nina'?
A: The cooling of the eastern Pacific waters, which generally brings a good monsoon.
Q: What are the main seasons of India?
A: Winter, summer, the southwest monsoon and the retreating monsoon (autumn).
Q: What is the 'October Heat'?
A: The hot and humid weather in October after the monsoon retreat.
Q: Which is the most widespread soil of India?
A: Alluvial soil.
Q: Which soil is formed by the weathering of the basaltic lava?
A: Black (regur) soil.
Q: Which soil is best for cotton cultivation?
A: Black (regur) soil.
Q: Where is black soil mainly found in India?
A: In the Deccan plateau region of Maharashtra, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh.
Q: Which soil is found in the desert regions of Rajasthan?
A: Arid (desert) soil.
Q: Which soil is found in the hilly areas of Assam?
A: Red and laterite soils.
Q: Which soil is formed in areas of high rainfall and high temperature?
A: Laterite soil.
Q: What is the main cause of soil erosion in Assam?
A: Floods, deforestation and shifting (jhum) cultivation.
Q: Which is the most fertile soil of the Brahmaputra valley?
A: The new alluvial soil.
Q: What is the 'khadar' soil?
A: New alluvial soil deposited by rivers in floodplains.
Q: What is the 'bangar' soil?
A: Old alluvial soil found at a higher level.
Q: Which state of India has the highest area under forest?
A: Madhya Pradesh.
Q: Which state of India has the highest forest cover percentage?
A: Mizoram.
Q: What is the 'western disturbances'?
A: Winter rainfall-causing winds from the Mediterranean region.
Q: Which parts of India receive winter rainfall from the western disturbances?
A: The north-western plains of Punjab, Haryana and western UP.
Q: What is the 'norwester' locally called in Assam?
A: Bordoisila.
Q: Which soil is suitable for tea cultivation?
A: Well-drained acidic soils of the foothill regions.
Q: What is the soil conservation method of building terraces?
A: Terrace cultivation on slopes.
Q: Which place receives rainfall from the retreating monsoon in India?
A: The eastern coast, especially Tamil Nadu.
Q: What is the effect of the Bay of Bengal branch of the monsoon on Assam?
A: It brings heavy rainfall to Assam and the North-East.
Q: Which is the driest state of India?
A: Rajasthan.

### Population, Density, Sex Ratio and Literacy | axomexam
