### Renewable and Non-Renewable Energy | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/indian-geography-sec/energy-renewable-nonrenewable-india/
Summary: Important questions on the renewable and non-renewable energy sources of India for Assam competitive exams. Covers ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What is renewable energy?
A: Energy from sources that are naturally replenished, like the sun and wind.
Q: What is non-renewable energy?
A: Energy from sources that cannot be replenished quickly, like coal and oil.
Q: Which is the largest source of power in India?
A: Thermal (coal-based) power.
Q: What is the share of thermal power in the total installed capacity of India?
A: About 60% to 70%.
Q: Which is the largest hydroelectric project of India?
A: The Koyna Hydroelectric Project in Maharashtra.
Q: Which is the largest hydropower station of India by installed capacity?
A: The Tehri Hydropower Project.
Q: What is the total installed capacity of the Tehri project?
A: About 2,400 MW.
Q: Which is the largest source of renewable energy in India?
A: Solar power.
Q: Which is the largest solar power park of the world?
A: The Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan.
Q: Which is the largest wind energy producing state of India?
A: Gujarat.
Q: Which state of India has the highest wind power capacity?
A: Gujarat, followed by Tamil Nadu.
Q: What is the wind energy capacity of India?
A: About 45,000 MW and growing.
Q: What is the 'National Solar Mission' of India?
A: A mission to promote solar power, targeting 100 GW of solar capacity.
Q: When was the National Solar Mission launched?
A: In 2010.
Q: What is the target of the solar capacity of India by 2030?
A: About 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity.
Q: Which is the largest nuclear power plant of India?
A: The Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant in Tamil Nadu.
Q: When was the first nuclear power plant of India commissioned?
A: The Tarapur plant in 1969.
Q: Where is the Tarapur nuclear power plant located?
A: In Maharashtra.
Q: What is the total nuclear power capacity of India?
A: About 7,000 MW.
Q: Which is the largest source of the renewable energy in the North-East India?
A: Hydropower.
Q: Which is the largest hydropower project of the North-East?
A: The Lower Subansiri project (about 2,000 MW).
Q: On which river is the Lower Subansiri project built?
A: The Subansiri river.
Q: What is the 'biogas'?
A: A renewable fuel produced from organic waste.
Q: What is the 'geothermal energy'?
A: Energy obtained from the heat of the earth.
Q: Where is the geothermal plant of India located?
A: At Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh and Tattapani in Chhattisgarh.
Q: What is the 'tidal energy'?
A: Energy generated from the rise and fall of the tides.
Q: Which is the main source of the hydroelectric power in India?
A: The rivers of the Himalayas and the Western Ghats.
Q: What is the share of the renewable energy in the total installed capacity of India?
A: About 30% to 35%.
Q: Which is the largest producer of the solar energy in the world?
A: China.
Q: Which is the largest solar state of India?
A: Rajasthan.
Q: What is the 'green energy'?
A: Energy from clean and renewable sources that do not pollute.
Q: What is the 'International Solar Alliance'?
A: An alliance of countries to promote solar energy, launched by India.
Q: When was the International Solar Alliance launched?
A: In 2015.
Q: Which is the main source of the thermal power in Assam?
A: Natural gas.
Q: What is the total renewable capacity of the North-East India?
A: About 1,500 MW and growing.

### Major Industrial Belts and International Borders | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/indian-geography-sec/industrial-belts-borders-frontiers-india/
Summary: Important questions on the major industrial belts and the international borders of India for Assam competitive exams. Practice for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What is an industrial belt?
A: A region where industries are concentrated due to favourable factors.
Q: Which is the oldest industrial belt of India?
A: The Hooghly industrial belt of West Bengal.
Q: Which is the most important industrial belt of India?
A: The Mumbai-Pune industrial belt.
Q: What are the main factors for the location of an industry?
A: Raw material, power, labour, transport and market.
Q: Which is the largest industrial belt of India by area?
A: The Chhotanagpur industrial belt.
Q: Which is the most important textile producing state of India?
A: Gujarat.
Q: Which is the largest producer of cotton textiles in India?
A: Gujarat.
Q: Which city is called the 'Manchester of India'?
A: Ahmedabad.
Q: Which is the largest producer of the iron and steel in India?
A: Odisha.
Q: Which is the oldest iron and steel plant of India?
A: The Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) at Jamshedpur.
Q: When was the Jamshedpur steel plant established?
A: In 1907.
Q: Where is the Bhilai steel plant located?
A: In Chhattisgarh.
Q: Where is the Bokaro steel plant located?
A: In Jharkhand.

A: In Odisha.
Q: Where is the Durgapur steel plant located?
A: In West Bengal.
Q: Which is the only steel plant of South India?
A: The Visakhapatnam Steel Plant in Andhra Pradesh.
Q: Where is the Salem steel plant located?
A: In Tamil Nadu.
Q: Which is the largest industrial city of India?
A: Mumbai.
Q: Which is the 'Silicon Valley of India'?
A: Bengaluru (Bangalore) in Karnataka.
Q: Which is the 'Detroit of India'?
A: Chennai, for its automobile industry.
Q: Which city is known as the 'steel city of India'?
A: Jamshedpur.
Q: Which is the largest industrial belt of the South India?
A: The Chennai-Bengaluru-Coimbatore belt.
Q: Which is the largest producer of silk in India?
A: Karnataka.

A: West Bengal.
Q: Which is the largest producer of sugar in India?
A: Uttar Pradesh.
Q: Which is the largest industrial belt of the North-East India?
A: The Guwahati industrial area of Assam.
Q: Which is the largest industry of Assam?
A: The tea industry.
Q: Which is the largest agro-based industry of India?
A: The cotton textile industry.
Q: Which is the largest mineral-based industry of India?
A: The iron and steel industry.
Q: Which is the largest producer of the chemicals in India?
A: Gujarat.
Q: Which is the largest producer of the fertilizer in India?
A: Gujarat.
Q: Which is the largest producer of the cement in India?
A: Rajasthan.
Q: Which is the largest producer of the electronics in India?
A: Tamil Nadu.
Q: Which is the largest producer of the automobile in India?
A: Maharashtra.
Q: Which is the 'poultry capital of India'?
A: Namakkal in Tamil Nadu.
Q: How many countries share a land border with India?
A: Seven countries.
Q: Which are the countries sharing a land border with India?
A: Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Afghanistan.
Q: Which is the longest international border of India?
A: The India-Bangladesh border.
Q: What is the length of the India-Bangladesh border?
A: About 4,096 kilometres.
Q: Which is the second longest international border of India?
A: The India-China border.
Q: What is the length of the India-China border?
A: About 3,488 kilometres.
Q: What is the total length of the land border of India?
A: About 15,200 kilometres.
Q: What is the length of the India-Pakistan border?
A: About 3,323 kilometres.
Q: What is the length of the India-Nepal border?
A: About 1,751 kilometres.
Q: What is the length of the India-Bhutan border?
A: About 699 kilometres.
Q: What is the length of the India-Myanmar border?
A: About 1,643 kilometres.
Q: Which Indian states share the border with Myanmar?
A: Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram.
Q: Which Indian states share the border with Bangladesh?
A: West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram and the union territory of the Andaman & Nicobar (maritime).
Q: Which Indian states share the border with Bhutan?
A: Sikkim, West Bengal, Assam and Arunachal Pradesh.
Q: Which Indian states share the border with China?
A: Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh.
Q: Which Indian states share the border with Nepal?
A: Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and Sikkim.
Q: Which Indian states share the border with Pakistan?
A: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab and Jammu & Kashmir.
Q: Which is the 'Line of Actual Control' (LAC)?
A: The de facto border between India and China.
Q: What is the 'Line of Control' (LOC)?
A: The de facto border between India and Pakistan in Kashmir.
Q: What is the 'Radcliffe Line'?
A: The boundary line between India and Pakistan drawn in 1947.
Q: What is the 'Durand Line'?
A: The boundary line between Afghanistan and Pakistan (once relevant for India).
Q: What is the 'McMahon Line'?
A: The border line between India and China in the Eastern sector.
Q: Which pass is the tri-junction of India, China and Myanmar?
A: The Diphu pass (in the eastern end of the McMahon Line).
Q: Which is the tri-junction of India, China and Nepal?
A: The Lipulekh pass.
Q: Which is the tri-junction of India, Bangladesh and Myanmar?
A: The junction near the Mizoram-Tripura-Bangladesh area.
Q: Which Indian state has the longest international border?
A: West Bengal (with Bangladesh).
Q: Which Indian state has the longest border with China?
A: Arunachal Pradesh.
Q: What is the length of the India-Afghanistan border?
A: About 106 kilometres (claimed via the Wakhan corridor).
Q: Which is the nearest sea route border of India?
A: The maritime borders with Sri Lanka, Maldives, Indonesia and Thailand.
Q: Which country has a maritime border with India?
A: Sri Lanka, Maldives, Indonesia, Thailand, Myanmar and Bangladesh.
Q: What is the total length of the coastline including the islands of India?
A: About 7,516.6 kilometres.
Q: Which is the narrowest point between India and Sri Lanka?
A: The Palk Strait.
Q: Which is the point separating the Gulf of Mannar from the Palk Bay?
A: The Adam's Bridge (Rama Setu).
Q: Which island of India is the closest to Sri Lanka?
A: The Dhanushkodi point in Rameswaram.
Q: Which is the southernmost tip of the Indian mainland?
A: Kanyakumari (Cape Comorin).

### Minerals: Iron, Coal, Petroleum and Bauxite | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/indian-geography-sec/minerals-iron-coal-petroleum-bauxite-india/
Summary: Important questions on the minerals of India - iron, coal, petroleum and bauxite - for Assam competitive exams. Covers ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What is a mineral?
A: A naturally occurring inorganic substance with a definite chemical composition.
Q: What are the two types of minerals?
A: Metallic and non-metallic minerals.
Q: Which is the largest producer of iron ore in India?
A: Odisha.

A: Magnetite.

A: Hematite.

A: In the Bastar district of Chhattisgarh.
Q: What is the total reserve of iron ore in India?
A: About 33 billion tonnes.
Q: Which is the largest producer of coal in India?
A: Jharkhand.
Q: Which is the largest coal field of India?
A: The Jharia coal field in Jharkhand.
Q: What is the oldest coal field of India?
A: The Raniganj coal field in West Bengal.
Q: Which is the largest coal producing company of India?
A: Coal India Limited (CIL).
Q: When was Coal India Limited established?
A: In 1975.
Q: What is the rank of India in the coal production of the world?
A: Second, after China.
Q: Which is the highest grade of coal?
A: Anthracite.
Q: What is the 'coking coal'?
A: Coal that can be converted into coke, used in the iron and steel industry.
Q: Which is the largest producer of petroleum in India?
A: Rajasthan (followed by Gujarat and Assam).
Q: Which is the oldest oil field of India?

A: The Mumbai High offshore field.

A: In 1974.
Q: Which is the oldest oil refinery of India?
A: The Digboi refinery in Assam.
Q: What is the total crude oil production of India?
A: About 30 million tonnes per year.
Q: Which state of India has the largest reserve of bauxite?
A: Odisha.
Q: Which is the largest bauxite producing state of India?
A: Odisha.
Q: What is bauxite?
A: An ore of aluminium.
Q: Which is the largest bauxite mine of India?
A: The Panchpatmali mine in Odisha.
Q: Which state of India is the largest producer of aluminium?
A: Odisha.
Q: Which is the largest producer of manganese in India?
A: Odisha.
Q: What is the use of manganese?
A: In the making of steel and alloys.
Q: Which is the largest producer of limestone in India?
A: Madhya Pradesh.
Q: Which is the largest producer of gold in India?
A: Karnataka.
Q: Which is the oldest gold mine of India?
A: The Kolar gold field in Karnataka.
Q: What is the 'mica' used for?
A: In the electrical and electronic industries.
Q: Which is the largest producer of mica in India?
A: Jharkhand.
Q: Which state of India has the largest reserve of the uranium?
A: Jharkhand.

Summary: Important questions on the national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves of India for Assam competitive exams. Covers ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: Which is the largest national park of India?
A: Hemis National Park in Ladakh.
Q: Which is the oldest national park of India?

A: The Jim Corbett Tiger Reserve.
Q: Which sanctuary of India is famous for the wild ass?
A: The Wild Ass Sanctuary in Gujarat (Kutch).
Q: Which sanctuary of India is known for the migratory birds?
A: The Keoladeo Ghana National Park (Bharatpur) in Rajasthan.
Q: Which national park of Assam is known as the 'Big Five' habitat?
A: The Manas National Park.
Q: Which is the only floating national park of the world?
A: The Keibul Lamjao National Park in Manipur.
Q: Which deer is protected in the Keibul Lamjao National Park?
A: The Sangai (Brow-antlered deer).
Q: Which is the smallest national park of India?
A: The South Button Island National Park in the Andamans.
Q: Which national park of India is in the Andaman and Nicobar islands?
A: The Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park and the Campbell Bay National Park.
Q: Which is the largest wildlife sanctuary of India?
A: The Indian Wild Ass Sanctuary in Gujarat.
Q: Which biosphere reserve of India is in the Himalayas?

A: The Mudumalai National Park.

A: The Pabho Wildlife Sanctuary, declared in 1980.
Q: Which national park of India is known for the 'Birds Paradise'?
A: The Keoladeo National Park.
Q: Which national park of India is the habitat of the snow leopard?

### Himalayas, Plains, Plateau, Islands and Coasts | axomexam

Q: What is the total length of the Himalayas?
A: About 2,400 kilometres.
Q: What are the three main parallel ranges of the Himalayas?

A: The Indo-Gangetic plains.

A: Bhabar, Terai and the alluvial plains.
Q: Which is the largest river island in the world?
A: Majuli, in Assam.

A: Rajasthan.

A: About 3.28 million square kilometres.
Q: Which is the widest part of the Himalayas?
A: The Kashmir Himalayas, about 400 kilometres wide.
Q: Which is the narrowest part of the Himalayas?
A: The Assam Himalayas, about 100 to 200 kilometres wide.

A: The Nathu La pass in Sikkim.

### Rivers: Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra and Peninsular | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/indian-geography-sec/rivers-indus-ganga-brahmaputra-peninsular/
Summary: Important questions on the major rivers of India - Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra and the peninsular rivers - for Assam competitive exams. Relevant for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other government exams.
Q: Which is the longest river of India?
A: The Ganga, with a total length of about 2,525 kilometres.
Q: Which is the longest river of the world flowing through India?
A: The Indus river.
Q: Where does the Ganga originate?
A: From the Gangotri glacier in Uttarakhand.
Q: What is the name of the source stream of the Ganga?
A: Bhagirathi.
Q: At which place does the Alaknanda meet the Bhagirathi?
A: At Devprayag.
Q: Where does the Ganga fall into the sea?
A: Into the Bay of Bengal through the Sundarbans delta.
Q: Which is the longest tributary of the Ganga?
A: The Yamuna.
Q: Where does the Yamuna originate?
A: From the Yamunotri glacier in Uttarakhand.
Q: Which is the largest tributary of the Ganga by discharge?
A: The Son and the Ghaghara are major tributaries.
Q: Where does the Brahmaputra originate?
A: From the Chemayungdung glacier near Manasarovar in Tibet.
Q: What is the name of the Brahmaputra in Tibet?
A: Tsangpo.
Q: Through which region does the Brahmaputra enter India?
A: Through Arunachal Pradesh (at the Namcha Barwa area).
Q: What is the name of the Brahmaputra in Arunachal Pradesh?
A: Dihang (Siang).
Q: Which is the largest river of the Barak valley?
A: The Barak river.
Q: What is the name of the Barak river in Bangladesh?
A: Surma and later Meghna.
Q: Which is the longest peninsular river of India?
A: The Godavari, with a length of about 1,465 kilometres.
Q: Where does the Godavari originate?
A: From the Trimbakeshwar hills in Nashik, Maharashtra.
Q: Which is the second longest river of the Peninsular India?
A: The Krishna river.
Q: Where does the Krishna originate?
A: From Mahabaleshwar in Maharashtra.
Q: Which is the southernmost river of India?
A: The Kaveri river.
Q: Where does the Kaveri originate?
A: From Brahmagiri in the Western Ghats, Karnataka.
Q: Which river is known as the 'Ganga of the South'?
A: The Kaveri river.
Q: Which is the west-flowing major river of the Peninsular India?
A: The Narmada and the Tapi.
Q: Where does the Narmada originate?
A: From the Amarkantak plateau in Madhya Pradesh.
Q: Which is the river that flows through a rift valley in India?
A: The Narmada river.
Q: Which river forms the largest waterfall of India?
A: The Sharavati river forms the Jog falls.
Q: Which river is the longest tributary of the Brahmaputra in Assam?
A: The Subansiri river.
Q: Which is the major north-bank tributary of the Brahmaputra?
A: The Subansiri, Siang, Dibang, Lohit and the Manas.
Q: Which is the major south-bank tributary of the Brahmaputra?
A: The Kopili, Dihing, Dhansiri and the Burhidihing.
Q: Which river flows through the Mawsynram region of Meghalaya?
A: The Umiam river and its tributaries.
Q: Which river is called the 'Sorrow of Bengal'?
A: The Damodar river.
Q: Which river is called the 'Sorrow of Bihar'?
A: The Kosi river.
Q: Which river flows through the Thar desert?
A: The Luni river.
Q: Which is the longest river of the North-East India?
A: The Brahmaputra.
Q: Which river of India flows into the Arabian Sea?
A: The Narmada, Tapi, Sabarmati and the Mahi.

A: The Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly river system.
Q: Which is the National Waterway 2 of India?

### Natural Vegetation and Forest Types | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/indian-geography-sec/vegetation-forest-types-india/
Summary: Important questions on the natural vegetation and forest types of India for Assam competitive exams. Useful for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other Assam government exams.
Q: What is the total forest cover of India as per the latest State of Forest Report?
A: About 21.71% of the geographical area.
Q: What percentage of the forest cover does the tree cover add to India?
A: About 24.62% together (forest + tree cover).
Q: What are the major types of forests in India?
A: Tropical evergreen, tropical deciduous, thorn, montane, mangrove and littoral forests.
Q: Which forest type covers the largest area of India?
A: Tropical deciduous forests.
Q: What is the other name of the tropical deciduous forests?
A: Monsoon forests.
Q: What is the percentage of the tropical deciduous forests of the total forest area of India?
A: About 65% of the total forest area.
Q: Where are the tropical evergreen forests found in India?
A: In the Western Ghats, the North-East and the Andaman islands.
Q: Which is the main tree of the tropical deciduous forests?
A: Teak, Sal and Bamboo.
Q: Where are the thorn forests found in India?
A: In the semi-arid regions of Rajasthan, Gujarat and Punjab.
Q: What is the main tree of the thorn forests?
A: Kikar, Babul and Khair.
Q: Where are the mangrove forests found in India?
A: In the deltas and the coastal areas, especially the Sundarbans.
Q: Which is the largest mangrove forest of the world?
A: The Sundarbans.
Q: Which tree is the main species of the Sundarbans?
A: Sundari tree.
Q: What are the littoral forests?
A: Forests along the sea coasts, with salt-tolerant species.
Q: What is the montane forest?
A: Forests found at high altitudes in the Himalayas and the other mountains.
Q: What type of forest is found in the foothills of the Himalayas?
A: Tropical wet deciduous and semi-evergreen forests.
Q: Which type of forest is found in the Eastern Himalayan belt?
A: Sub-tropical and temperate forests, including rhododendron forests.
Q: What is the 'sacred groves' in the North-East?
A: Community-protected forest patches of the tribal people.
Q: What is the main vegetation of the 'Terai' region?
A: Tall grasses, swampy vegetation and sal forests.
Q: Which forest type is found around the Tropic of Cancer region?
A: Tropical dry deciduous and thorn forests.
Q: Which forest is known as the 'lungs of the Earth'?
A: The tropical rainforests, like the Amazon and the Dehing-Patkai.
Q: Which is the largest rainforest of India?
A: The Dehing-Patkai rainforest in Assam.
Q: Which forest of India is famous for the 'Hollong' trees?
A: The Jeypore rainforest of Assam.
Q: What is the cause of the decline of the forest area in the North-East?
A: Jhum cultivation, logging and encroachment.
Q: What is the 'Van Mahotsav'?
A: The tree plantation festival of India, celebrated in the first week of July.
Q: What is the National Forest Policy of India?
A: It aims to maintain at least one-third of the total land area under forest.
Q: What is the total recorded forest area of the North-East India?
A: More than 65% of the region is forested.
Q: Which state of the North-East has the lowest forest cover?
A: Assam, among the eight states of the region.
Q: Which is the main bamboo producing state of India?
A: Mizoram.
Q: What is the 'shifting cultivation' called in the North-East?
A: Jhum cultivation.
Q: Which forest type grows in the areas of 100 to 200 cm rainfall?
A: Moist deciduous forests.
Q: Which forest type grows in the areas of 50 to 100 cm rainfall?
A: Dry deciduous forests.
Q: Which is the most important tree of the evergreen forests of the Western Ghats?
A: Rosewood, Ebony and Mahogany.
Q: What is the 'sal' tree mainly used for?
A: For timber and railway sleepers.
Q: Which is the national tree of India?
A: The Banyan (Ficus benghalensis) tree.

### Atmosphere Layers, Winds and Cyclones | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/world-geography-sec/atmosphere-layers-winds-cyclones/
Summary: Important questions on the atmosphere layers, winds and cyclones for Assam competitive exams. Covers ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What is the atmosphere?
A: The blanket of gases surrounding the Earth.
Q: What is the main gas of the atmosphere?
A: Nitrogen (about 78%).
Q: What is the second most abundant gas of the atmosphere?
A: Oxygen (about 21%).
Q: What are the five layers of the atmosphere?
A: Troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere.
Q: Which is the lowest layer of the atmosphere?
A: The troposphere.
Q: In which layer do we live and weather occurs?
A: The troposphere.
Q: What is the average height of the troposphere?
A: About 13 to 14 kilometres.
Q: Which layer contains the ozone layer?
A: The stratosphere.
Q: What does the ozone layer protect us from?
A: From the harmful ultraviolet rays of the sun.
Q: In which layer does the temperature increase with height?
A: In the stratosphere and the thermosphere.
Q: In which layer do the meteors burn up?
A: The mesosphere.
Q: Which layer contains the ionosphere used for radio communication?
A: The thermosphere.
Q: Which is the uppermost layer of the atmosphere?
A: The exosphere.
Q: What is 'air pressure'?
A: The weight of the air pressing down on the Earth's surface.
Q: What are the permanent winds?
A: The trade winds, the westerlies and the polar easterlies.
Q: Which winds blow from the subtropical high to the equatorial low?
A: The trade winds.
Q: What are the trade winds called in the northern hemisphere?
A: The North-East trade winds.
Q: Which winds blow from the horse latitudes to the polar region?
A: The westerlies.
Q: What are the seasonal winds of India?
A: The monsoon winds.
Q: What is a cyclone?
A: A system of low pressure with strong winds rotating around a centre.
Q: What is the centre of a cyclone called?
A: The eye of the cyclone.
Q: What is the 'eye' of the cyclone?
A: The calm centre of the cyclone.
Q: What are the cyclones of the Pacific Ocean called?
A: Typhoons.
Q: What are the cyclones of the Atlantic Ocean called?
A: Hurricanes.
Q: What are the cyclones of the Indian Ocean called?
A: Cyclones.
Q: In which direction do the cyclones rotate in the northern hemisphere?
A: Anti-clockwise.
Q: What are the cyclones of the Bay of Bengal called?
A: Cyclonic storms.
Q: What is the main cause of the cyclone formation?
A: The warm ocean waters and the low pressure over the sea.
Q: What is the 'cyclone warning' system of India called?
A: The IMD cyclone warning system.
Q: What is the effect of the global warming on the cyclones?
A: It increases their frequency and intensity.

### Earth Layers, Plates and Volcanoes | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/geography/world-geography-sec/earth-layers-plates-volcanoes/
Summary: Important questions on the layers of the Earth, tectonic plates and volcanoes for Assam competitive exams. Practice for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: What are the three layers of the Earth?
A: The crust, the mantle and the core.
Q: What is the outermost layer of the Earth called?
A: The crust.
Q: What is the average thickness of the continental crust?
A: About 35 kilometres.
Q: What is the average thickness of the oceanic crust?
A: About 5 kilometres.
Q: Which layer of the Earth is the thickest?
A: The mantle.
Q: What is the thickness of the mantle?
A: About 2,900 kilometres.
Q: What is the innermost layer of the Earth?
A: The inner core.
Q: What is the inner core made of?
A: Solid iron and nickel.
Q: What is the radius of the Earth?
A: About 6,371 kilometres.
Q: What is the temperature of the Earth's core?
A: About 5,000 to 6,000 degrees Celsius.
Q: What is the 'lithosphere'?
A: The solid outer part of the Earth, including the crust and the upper mantle.
Q: What is the 'asthenosphere'?
A: The semi-molten layer of the upper mantle on which the plates move.
Q: Who proposed the theory of continental drift?
A: Alfred Wegener, in 1912.
Q: What is the 'Pangaea'?
A: The supercontinent that existed about 200 million years ago.
Q: How many major tectonic plates are there on the Earth?
A: Seven major plates.
Q: Which is the largest tectonic plate?
A: The Pacific plate.
Q: What is the 'ring of fire'?
A: The belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific Ocean.
Q: What happens at the convergent plate boundaries?
A: Plates collide, forming mountains, and causing earthquakes.
Q: What happens at the divergent plate boundaries?
A: Plates move apart, forming new crust and mid-oceanic ridges.
Q: What is a volcano?
A: An opening in the Earth's crust through which magma erupts.
Q: What is magma called when it reaches the surface?
A: Lava.
Q: What are the three types of volcanoes?
A: Active, dormant and extinct.
Q: What is a 'shield volcano'?
A: A broad volcano formed by low-viscosity lava, like Mauna Loa.
Q: What is a 'stratovolcano'?
A: A tall cone-shaped volcano made of layers of lava and ash.
Q: Which is the largest active volcano of the world?
A: Mauna Loa in Hawaii.
Q: What is the 'Mount Fuji'?
A: The highest active volcano of Japan, about 3,776 metres.
Q: Which is the highest volcano of the world?
A: Nevado Ojos del Salado, in the Andes.
Q: What is the 'mid-oceanic ridge'?
A: An underwater mountain range formed at the divergent boundaries.
Q: Which is the longest mountain range of the world?
A: The mid-oceanic ridge system (about 65,000 km), led by the Andes on land.
Q: What is the theory of plate tectonics?
A: The theory that the Earth's lithosphere is divided into moving plates.

Q: What is the scale used to measure the magnitude of an earthquake?
A: The Richter scale.
Q: What is the point of origin of an earthquake inside the Earth called?
A: The focus (hypocentre).
Q: What is the point on the surface directly above the focus called?
A: The epicentre.
Q: Which is the most earthquake-prone zone of India?
A: The North-Eastern region (Zone V).
Q: What is a tsunami?
A: A series of giant ocean waves caused by an underwater earthquake.
Q: What is the 'Richter scale'?

### Ancient Indian Art, Architecture & Literature | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/indian-history/ancient-indian-history-sec/ancient-art-arch-lit/
Summary: Schools of art, stupas, cave temples, temple styles and the great literature of ancient India. Relevant for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other government exams.
Q: Who originally built the famous Sanchi stupa?
A: Ashoka the Great, as a brick stupa.
Q: Which is the most famous and best-preserved stupa of India?
A: The Great Stupa at Sanchi (Madhya Pradesh).
Q: Which dynasty enlarged and renovated the Sanchi stupa?
A: The Sungas, who added the stone railing and the gateways.
Q: What are the four toranas (gateways) of Sanchi famous for?
A: Their exquisite narrative sculptures depicting Jataka stories.
Q: The sculptures of the Bharhut stupa belong to which period?
A: The Sunga period (2nd century BC).
Q: Which famous stupa of Andhra Pradesh was built in the Satavahana period?
A: The Amaravati stupa.
Q: Which school of art is known for its Greco-Roman influence?
A: The Gandhara school.
Q: Where did the Gandhara school of art flourish?
A: In the north-western region - Taxila, Peshawar and the Kabul valley.
Q: Which stone was used by the artists of the Gandhara school?
A: Grey-blue schist stone.
Q: Which school of art was indigenous and used red sandstone?
A: The Mathura school of art.
Q: Where was the Mathura school of art centred?
A: At Mathura (Uttar Pradesh).
Q: Which Kushan ruler patronised both the Gandhara and Mathura schools?
A: Kanishka.
Q: Which school of art flourished in the Andhra region?
A: The Amravati school (at Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda).
Q: What are the Ajanta caves famous for?
A: Their magnificent Buddhist paintings (frescoes) and sculptures.
Q: When were the Ajanta caves discovered by the British?
A: In 1819, by a British army officer John Smith.
Q: Which painting of Ajanta cave 1 is world-famous?
A: The Padmapani (Bodhisattva) painting.
Q: Where are the Bagh caves located and what are they famous for?
A: In Madhya Pradesh, famous for their ancient Buddhist paintings.
Q: Which cave in Tamil Nadu is famous for its Jaina paintings?
A: The Sittanavasal cave.
Q: Who built the Kailasa temple at Ellora?
A: The Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna I (8th century AD).
Q: What makes the Kailasa temple at Ellora unique?
A: It is a monolithic rock-cut temple - the largest such temple in the world, carved out of a single rock.
Q: Where is the famous Trimurti sculpture located?
A: In the Elephanta caves (near Mumbai).
Q: What does the Elephanta Trimurti depict?
A: The three-faced figure of Shiva (Mahesh), showing his three aspects.
Q: Which are the two main styles of Indian temple architecture?
A: The Nagara style (northern) and the Dravida style (southern); the Vesara is the hybrid Chalukyan style.
Q: Which Gupta temple at Deogarh represents the Nagara style?
A: The Dashavatara temple.
Q: Which style does the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram represent?
A: The Dravida style.
Q: What is the basic feature of a Dravida temple?
A: The pyramidal storeyed tower called the Vimana, above the sanctum.
Q: Which Jaina caves of Odisha are associated with king Kharavela?
A: The Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves.
Q: Who wrote the Ramayana?
A: Maharshi Valmiki.
Q: Why is the Ramayana called the 'Adi Kavya'?
A: Because it is regarded as the first poem (Kavya) of Sanskrit literature.
Q: Who wrote the Mahabharata?
A: Maharshi Vyasa (Vedavyasa).
Q: How many parvas does the Mahabharata contain?
A: Eighteen (18) parvas.
Q: What is the Mahabharata sometimes called?
A: The fifth Veda, because of its immense size and importance.
Q: Who wrote the Natyashastra, the treatise on drama?
A: Bharata Muni.
Q: Who wrote the Ashtadhyayi, the famous Sanskrit grammar?
A: Panini.
Q: Who is the traditional author of the Manusmriti?
A: Manu.
Q: What are the Jataka tales?
A: Buddhist stories about the previous births of the Buddha, which teach moral lessons.
Q: Who wrote the Arthashastra?
A: Kautilya (Chanakya).
Q: Who wrote the Charaka Samhita?
A: Charaka, the ancient physician.
Q: Who is regarded as the father of Indian surgery?
A: Sushruta.
Q: Which text did Sushruta write?
A: The Sushruta Samhita, dealing with surgery.
Q: Who wrote the Panchatantra?
A: Vishnusharma.
Q: What is the Sangam literature?
A: Ancient Tamil literature composed in the assemblies (Sangams) at Madurai, between about 300 BC and 300 AD.
Q: What are the two famous Tamil epics?
A: Shilappadikaram by Ilango Adigal and Manimekalai by Sattanar.
Q: Who wrote the Mrichchakatika (The Little Clay Cart)?
A: King Shudraka.
Q: Who wrote the Swapnavasavadatta?
A: Bhasa, one of the earliest Sanskrit dramatists.
Q: Which is the most celebrated play of Kalidasa?
A: Abhijnanasakuntalam.
Q: Who wrote the Kiratarjuniya?
A: Bharavi.
Q: Who wrote the Dashakumaracharita?
A: Dandin.
Q: Which great Indian contribution in mathematics is world-renowned?
A: The invention of the zero and the decimal place-value system.
Q: Who wrote the Brahmasphutasiddhanta?
A: Brahmagupta (in 628 AD).
Q: Who wrote the Gita Govinda?
A: Jayadeva, a poet of the 12th century, depicting the love of Krishna and Radha.

### Gupta Empire | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/indian-history/ancient-indian-history-sec/gupta-empire/
Summary: The Golden Age of India - Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, Chandragupta II, culture, literature and decline. Practice for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: Who founded the Gupta dynasty?
A: Chandragupta I (ruled about 319-335 AD).
Q: When did the Gupta era begin?
A: In 319-320 AD, with the accession of Chandragupta I.
Q: Whom did Chandragupta I marry?
A: Kumaradevi, a princess of the Lichchhavis.
Q: What title did Chandragupta I assume?
A: Maharajadhiraja (king of kings).
Q: Who was the greatest ruler of the Gupta dynasty?
A: Samudragupta (335-380 AD).
Q: Who described Samudragupta as the 'Napoleon of India'?
A: The historian V. A. Smith.
Q: Which inscription records the conquests of Samudragupta?
A: The Allahabad Pillar inscription (Prayag Prashasti).
Q: Who composed the Prayag Prashasti?
A: Harishena, the court poet of Samudragupta.
Q: How did Samudragupta treat the kings of Aryavarta (the north)?
A: He uprooted nine kings and annexed their kingdoms.
Q: How did Samudragupta treat the kings of Dakshinapatha (the south)?
A: He defeated twelve kings but restored their kingdoms, following the policy of Dharma-vijaya.
Q: Which sacrifice did Samudragupta perform?
A: The Ashvamedha sacrifice, to proclaim his supremacy.
Q: What title did Samudragupta take because of his poetic talent?
A: Kaviraja (king of poets).
Q: Which types of coins did Samudragupta issue?
A: Gold coins of many types - the standard, archer, battle-axe and Ashvamedha types.
Q: Who succeeded Samudragupta?
A: His son Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya).
Q: Which Saka ruler was defeated by Chandragupta II?
A: Rudrasimha III, ending the Saka rule in western India.
Q: What title did Chandragupta II assume?
A: Vikramaditya.
Q: Which Chinese pilgrim visited India during the reign of Chandragupta II?
A: Fahien (Fa-Hien), in about 399-414 AD.
Q: What did Fahien write?
A: Fo-Kwo-Ki (A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms).
Q: What did Fahien observe about the Gupta administration?
A: The people were prosperous and happy; there were no severe punishments and no poll tax.
Q: What is the iron pillar at Mehrauli (Delhi) famous for?
A: Its rust-resistant iron; it bears an inscription of Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya).
Q: Who were the Navaratnas (Nine Gems) of the court of Chandragupta II?
A: Nine great scholars including Kalidasa, Varahamihira, Aryabhata, Dhanvantari, Amarasimha and Vararuchi.
Q: Which great poet adorned the court of Chandragupta II?
A: Kalidasa.
Q: Which famous play did Kalidasa write?
A: Abhijnanasakuntalam (The Recognition of Shakuntala).
Q: What are the other major works of Kalidasa?
A: Raghuvamsha, Kumarasambhava, Meghaduta, Vikramorvasiyam and Malavikagnimitra.
Q: Who wrote the Panchatantra?
A: Vishnusharma.
Q: Who wrote the Kamasutra?
A: Vatsyayana.
Q: Who wrote the Amarakosha (the famous Sanskrit lexicon)?
A: Amarasimha.
Q: Who composed the Aryabhatiya?
A: Aryabhata, in 499 AD.
Q: Who wrote the Brihatsamhita?
A: Varahamihira.
Q: Which university was founded by Kumaragupta I?
A: The Nalanda University (Bihar).
Q: Who repulsed the first Huna invasion?
A: Skandagupta.
Q: Who was the last great ruler of the Gupta dynasty?
A: Skandagupta (455-467 AD).
Q: What title did Skandagupta assume?
A: Vikramaditya.
Q: Which Gupta ruler repaired the Sudarshana lake?
A: Skandagupta, through his governor Parnadatta, as recorded in the Junagadh inscription.
Q: Which inscription provides the first evidence of sati in India?
A: The Eran inscription of 510 AD (of Bhanugupta).
Q: What was the administrative structure of the Gupta empire?
A: The empire was divided into Bhukti (province), Vishaya (district) and Grama (village); the Vishayapati headed a district.
Q: Who was the head of a Gupta district called?
A: Vishayapati.
Q: What were the land grants to Brahmins called in the Gupta period?
A: Agrahara grants (and Devagraha for temples).
Q: Which type of gold coins did the Guptas issue?
A: Gold dinara coins.
Q: Which period is called the 'Golden Age' of ancient India?
A: The Gupta period (4th-6th century AD).
Q: Why is the Gupta age called the 'Golden Age'?
A: Because of remarkable progress in art, architecture, literature, science, and all-round prosperity.
Q: Which rock-cut caves belong to the Gupta period?
A: The Udayagiri caves (Vidisha) and the early Ajanta paintings.
Q: Which famous temple at Deogarh belongs to the Gupta period?
A: The Dashavatara temple.
Q: Which brick temple of the Gupta period is located at Bhitargaon?
A: The Bhitargaon temple, built of brick with terracotta panels.
Q: Which religion was mainly revived under the Guptas?
A: Brahmanism, especially Vaishnavism and Shaivism.
Q: What were the main reasons for the decline of the Gupta empire?
A: Huna invasions, weak successors, the rise of feudatories and administrative decline.
Q: Which Huna rulers weakened the Gupta empire in its last phase?
A: Toramana and his son Mihirakula.
Q: Which city was the capital of the Gupta empire?
A: Pataliputra (with Ujjain as an important cultural centre).
Q: Who is regarded as the greatest Sanskrit dramatist of ancient India?
A: Kalidasa.
Q: Which Gupta ruler's coins depict him as a musician playing the veena?
A: Samudragupta (the 'lyrist' type of his gold coins).

A: Yes. All questions, answers and explanations for Gupta Empire are completely free, with no login or payment required.

A: Yes. Every question and answer in this topic is bilingual, so you can practise in Assamese and English.

A: This page contains 50 practice questions, and new questions are added regularly.

### Indus Valley Civilization | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/indian-history/ancient-indian-history-sec/indus-valley-civilization/
Summary: India's first urban civilization - Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, town planning, seals, script and decline. Relevant for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other government exams.
Q: What is another name of the Indus Valley Civilization?
A: Harappan Civilization, named after the site of Harappa.
Q: Which is considered the first urban civilization of India?
A: The Indus Valley (Harappan) Civilization.
Q: When and by whom was Harappa first excavated?
A: In 1921 by Daya Ram Sahni.
Q: When and by whom was Mohenjo-daro discovered?
A: In 1922 by R. D. Banerjee.
Q: Who announced the discovery of the Indus Valley Civilization in 1924?
A: John Marshall, the then Director General of the Archaeological Survey of India.
Q: Who first used the name 'Indus Valley Civilization'?
A: John Marshall.
Q: What is the generally accepted date of the Mature Harappan phase?
A: About 2500 BC to 1750 BC.
Q: On which river is Harappa situated?
A: The Ravi river (Punjab, Pakistan).
Q: On which river is Mohenjo-daro situated?
A: The Indus river (Sindh, Pakistan).
Q: Which is the largest site of the Harappan civilization?
A: Mohenjo-daro.
Q: Which is the largest Harappan site located in India?
A: Rakhigarhi (Haryana).
Q: Which is the westernmost site of the Harappan civilization?
A: Sutkagendor (Balochistan, Pakistan).
Q: Which is the easternmost site of the Harappan civilization?
A: Alamgirpur (Uttar Pradesh).
Q: Which is the northernmost site of the Harappan civilization?
A: Manda (Jammu and Kashmir).
Q: Which is the southernmost site of the Harappan civilization?
A: Daimabad (Maharashtra).
Q: Which Harappan site is famous for its dockyard?
A: Lothal (Gujarat).
Q: What was the main building material of the Harappan cities?
A: Burnt (baked) bricks, usually in the ratio 4:2:1.
Q: What were the main features of Harappan town planning?
A: Grid pattern, streets crossing at right angles, and covered drainage system.
Q: Which structure of Mohenjo-daro proves the water management skill of the Harappans?
A: The Great Bath.
Q: With what is the 'Great Granary' associated?
A: Public granaries built at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro for storing grain.
Q: At which site was the bronze 'Dancing Girl' statue found?
A: Mohenjo-daro.
Q: At which site was the steatite 'Priest King' statue found?
A: Mohenjo-daro.
Q: At which site was the famous 'Pashupati seal' discovered?
A: Mohenjo-daro.
Q: What does the 'Pashupati seal' depict?
A: A three-faced seated figure surrounded by animals, identified as a proto-Shiva.
Q: What was the nature of the Harappan script?
A: It was pictographic and has not yet been deciphered.
Q: In which direction was the Harappan script generally written?
A: Generally from right to left.
Q: Which material was mainly used for making Harappan seals?
A: Steatite (soapstone).
Q: What was the main purpose of the Harappan seals?
A: Trade purposes and sealing of goods; they also served as amulets.
Q: What system of weights did the Harappans use?
A: The binary system - 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32... using cubical chert weights.
Q: Which metal was unknown to the Harappan people?
A: Iron.
Q: Which metals were most commonly used by the Harappans?
A: Copper and bronze; gold and silver were also known.
Q: The Harappans were the first in the world to cultivate which crop?
A: Cotton.
Q: Which were the two main crops of the Harappans?
A: Wheat and barley; rice was also grown at Lothal and Rangpur.
Q: At which Harappan sites was evidence of rice cultivation found?
A: Lothal and Rangpur (Gujarat).
Q: Which animal was not known to the Harappans?
A: The horse.
Q: Which site provides the earliest evidence of a ploughed field?
A: Kalibangan (Rajasthan).
Q: In which state and on which river is Kalibangan situated?
A: In Rajasthan, on the banks of the Ghaggar river.
Q: Which Harappan site is famous for its water reservoirs and signboard?
A: Dholavira (Gujarat).
Q: Where is Dholavira located?
A: On the Khadir Bet island in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat.
Q: Which Harappan site is famous as a bead-making centre?
A: Chanhu-daro (Sindh, Pakistan).
Q: At which site was a terracotta model of a ship found?
A: Lothal.
Q: Who claimed to have found horse bones at Surkotada?
A: A. K. Sharma.
Q: At which site was a bronze model of a chariot found?
A: Daimabad (Maharashtra).
Q: What were the main occupations of the Harappan people?
A: Agriculture, animal husbandry, trade, crafts and industry.
Q: With which foreign land did the Harappans trade?
A: Mesopotamia (modern Iraq); the Indus region was called 'Meluhha' there.
Q: What is 'Meluhha' in Mesopotamian records?
A: The name given to the Indus region in Mesopotamian inscriptions.
Q: What evidence proves the foreign trade of the Harappans?
A: Harappan seals found in Mesopotamia and Mesopotamian seals and weights at Harappan sites.
Q: Did the Harappans have temples?
A: No evidence of a temple or idol worship has been found.
Q: Which animals are commonly depicted on the Harappan seals?
A: Humped bull, unicorn, elephant, rhinoceros and tiger.
Q: What was the general plan of the Harappan cities?
A: A higher citadel in the west and a lower town in the east.
Q: What do the covered drains of Mohenjo-daro indicate?
A: An advanced system of sanitation and public hygiene.
Q: Which deities were mainly worshipped by the Harappans?
A: The Mother Goddess and a male deity (proto-Shiva).
Q: What are the possible reasons for the decline of the Harappan civilization?
A: Floods, climate change, drying up of the Ghaggar and ecological factors; the old 'Aryan invasion' theory is now rejected.

A: This page contains 53 practice questions, and new questions are added regularly.

### Rise of Jainism & Buddhism | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/indian-history/ancient-indian-history-sec/jainism-buddhism/
Summary: Life of Mahavira and Buddha, their teachings, councils, sects and sacred texts. Relevant for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other government exams.
Q: Who was the founder of Jainism in its present form (the 24th Tirthankara)?
A: Mahavira (Vardhamana).
Q: How many Tirthankaras are there in Jainism?
A: 24 Tirthankaras.
Q: Who was the first Tirthankara of Jainism?
A: Rishabhanatha (Adinatha).
Q: Who was the 23rd Tirthankara of Jainism?
A: Parshvanatha.
Q: Where was Mahavira born?
A: At Kundagrama (Kundalpur), near Vaishali in Bihar.
Q: What was the childhood name of Mahavira?
A: Vardhamana.
Q: Who were the parents of Mahavira?
A: Father Siddhartha and mother Trishala.
Q: To which clan did Mahavira belong?
A: The Jnatrika clan, a Kshatriya clan of the Lichchhavis.
Q: At what age did Mahavira renounce the world?
A: At the age of 30.
Q: What is 'Kevala Jnana' in Jainism?
A: The supreme and perfect knowledge attained by Mahavira.
Q: Where did Mahavira attain Kaivalya (enlightenment)?
A: On the bank of the Rijupalika river under a Sal tree, near Jambhikagrama.
Q: Where did Mahavira deliver his first sermon?
A: At Pava.
Q: Where did Mahavira die?
A: At Pava (Bihar).
Q: At what age did Mahavira die?
A: At 72; the Jaina tradition places his death in 527 BC.
Q: What are the five vows (Anuvratas) of Jainism?
A: Ahimsa (non-violence), Satya (truth), Asteya (non-stealing), Brahmacharya (celibacy) and Aparigraha (non-possession).
Q: Which vow did Mahavira add to the four vows of Parshvanatha?
A: Brahmacharya (celibacy).
Q: What are the three Jewels (Triratna) of Jainism?
A: Right faith (Samyak Darshana), right knowledge (Samyak Jnana) and right conduct (Samyak Charitra).
Q: Which doctrine of Jainism says that reality is many-sided?
A: Anekantavada.
Q: Which doctrine of Jainism is the theory of conditional predication?
A: Syadvada.
Q: Why was Mahavira called 'Nirgrantha'?
A: Because he was free from all bonds and attachments.
Q: Who was the chief disciple (Ganadhara) of Mahavira?
A: Indrabhuti Gautama.
Q: In which language were the Jaina canon (Svetambara Agamas) written?
A: In Ardhamagadhi Prakrit.
Q: What are the two main sects of Jainism?
A: Digambara (sky-clad) and Svetambara (white-clad).
Q: At which council did the Digambara-Svetambara split take place?
A: At the Pataliputra council (3rd century BC), under the leadership of Bhadrabahu.
Q: Who led the Jaina monks from Magadha to Karnataka?
A: Bhadrabahu.
Q: Where was the first Jaina council held?
A: At Pataliputra, under Sthulabhadra.
Q: Where and when was the second Jaina council held?
A: At Vallabhi (Gujarat), in the 5th century AD.
Q: Which famous Jaina statue is located at Shravanabelagola?
A: The Gommateshwara (Bahubali) statue.
Q: Who was the founder of Buddhism?
A: Gautama Buddha.
Q: When and where was Gautama Buddha born?
A: Around 563 BC at Lumbini, near Kapilavastu (Nepal).
Q: Who were the parents of Gautama Buddha?
A: King Suddhodana and Queen Mahamaya.
Q: To which clan did Buddha belong?
A: The Shakya (Sakya) clan.
Q: What were the names of Buddha's wife and son?
A: Yashodhara and Rahul.
Q: At what age did Buddha leave his home?
A: At the age of 29.
Q: What is the 'Mahabhinishkramana'?
A: The Great Renunciation - Buddha's departure from his home in search of truth.
Q: Where did Buddha attain enlightenment?
A: At Bodh Gaya, under the Bodhi (peepal) tree on the bank of the river Niranjana.
Q: Where did Buddha deliver his first sermon?
A: At Sarnath (Deer Park), near Varanasi.
Q: What is the first sermon of Buddha called?
A: Dharmachakra Pravartana (Turning of the Wheel of Law).
Q: Where did Buddha die?
A: At Kushinagar (Uttar Pradesh).
Q: What is the 'Mahaparinirvana'?
A: The final passing away of Buddha at Kushinagar at the age of 80 (about 483 BC).
Q: Who offered Buddha his last meal?
A: Chunda, a blacksmith.
Q: What are the Four Noble Truths of Buddhism?
A: Dukkha (suffering), Samudaya (cause of suffering), Nirodha (cessation) and Magga (the path to cessation).
Q: What are the components of the Eightfold Path?
A: Right views, right resolve, right speech, right conduct, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration.
Q: What is the 'Middle Path' in Buddhism?
A: The path that avoids the extremes of self-indulgence and self-mortification.
Q: What are the Three Jewels (Triratna) of Buddhism?
A: Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha.
Q: Who were the two chief disciples of Buddha?
A: Sariputta and Moggallana.
Q: Who was the personal attendant of Buddha?
A: Ananda.
Q: What are the Tripitakas?
A: The three baskets - Vinaya Pitaka (rules of discipline), Sutta Pitaka (sermons) and Abhidhamma Pitaka (philosophy).
Q: In which language were the Tripitakas written?
A: In Pali.
Q: Where and under whom was the first Buddhist council held?
A: At Rajgriha in 483 BC, under Mahakassapa, during the reign of Ajatashatru.
Q: Where and under whom was the second Buddhist council held?
A: At Vaishali in 383 BC, under Sabakami; it led to the Sthaviravada-Mahasanghika split.
Q: Where and under whom was the third Buddhist council held?
A: At Pataliputra in about 250 BC, under Moggaliputta Tissa, patronised by Ashoka.
Q: Where and under whom was the fourth Buddhist council held?
A: At Kashmir in the 1st century AD, under Vasumitra, patronised by Kanishka.
Q: Which Mahayana philosopher founded the Madhyamika school?
A: Nagarjuna.
Q: Which Buddhist text records the dialogue between King Milinda (Menander) and Nagasena?
A: The Milindapanha (Questions of Milinda).

A: Yes. All questions, answers and explanations for Rise of Jainism & Buddhism are completely free, with no login or payment required.

A: Yes. Every question and answer in this topic is bilingual, so you can practise in Assamese and English.

A: This page contains 55 practice questions, and new questions are added regularly.

### Mahajanapadas & Magadha Empire | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/indian-history/ancient-indian-history-sec/mahajanapadas-magadha/
Summary: The sixteen Mahajanapadas and the rise of Magadha - Haryanka, Sisunaga and Nanda dynasties. Relevant for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other government exams.
Q: How many Mahajanapadas were there in ancient India?
A: Sixteen (16).
Q: Which were the sixteen Mahajanapadas?
A: Anga, Magadha, Kasi, Kosala, Vajji, Malla, Chedi, Vatsa, Kuru, Panchala, Matsya, Surasena, Ashmaka, Avanti, Gandhara and Kamboja.
Q: Which Mahajanapadas were republican (gana-sangha) in nature?
A: Vajji and Malla.
Q: What was the initial capital of Magadha?
A: Girivraja (Rajagriha).
Q: What was the capital of the Anga Mahajanapada?
A: Champa.
Q: What was the capital of the Kasi Mahajanapada?
A: Varanasi.
Q: What was the capital of the Kosala Mahajanapada?
A: Sravasti (with Ayodhya as a secondary capital).
Q: What was the capital of the Vajji confederacy?
A: Vaishali.
Q: What was the capital of the Vatsa Mahajanapada?
A: Kaushambi.
Q: What was the capital of the Avanti Mahajanapada?
A: Ujjaini (earlier Mahishmati).
Q: What was the capital of the Gandhara Mahajanapada?
A: Taxila (Takshashila).
Q: What was the capital of the Surasena Mahajanapada?
A: Mathura.
Q: What was the capital of the Matsya Mahajanapada?
A: Viratanagara (Bairat).
Q: What was the capital of the Panchala Mahajanapada?
A: Kampilya.
Q: Which were the two towns of the Malla republic?
A: Kusinara (Kushinagar) and Pava.
Q: Which four Mahajanapadas were the most powerful?
A: Magadha, Kosala, Avanti and Vatsa.
Q: Which Mahajanapada ultimately became the most powerful in north India?
A: Magadha.
Q: What were the main reasons for the rise of Magadha?
A: Strategic location, fertile Gangetic plains, iron mines in the Rajmahal hills, elephants, and strong ambitious rulers.
Q: Which was the first ruling dynasty of Magadha in the 6th century BC?
A: The Haryanka dynasty.
Q: Who was the founder of the Haryanka dynasty?
A: Bimbisara.
Q: By what other name was Bimbisara known?
A: Shrenika.
Q: Where was the capital of Bimbisara?
A: Rajagriha (Girivraja).
Q: How did Bimbisara strengthen his position?
A: Through matrimonial alliances - marrying Kosala Devi, the Lichchhavi princess Chellana and a princess of Madra.
Q: Who was the contemporary ruler of Magadha during the time of Buddha?
A: Bimbisara and later his son Ajatashatru.
Q: Who was the son of Bimbisara who imprisoned and killed his father?
A: Ajatashatru.
Q: By what other name was Ajatashatru known?
A: Kunika.
Q: Against which confederacy did Ajatashatru fight a prolonged war?
A: The Vajji (Lichchhavi) confederacy of Vaishali.
Q: Which two new weapons did Ajatashatru use against the Vajjis?
A: The Mahasilakantaka (catapult) and the Rathamushala (a mace-fitted chariot).
Q: Which ruler built a fort at Pataliputra?
A: Ajatashatru built the fort at Pataligrama (later Pataliputra).
Q: Which ruler shifted the capital of Magadha to Pataliputra?
A: Udayin, the son of Ajatashatru.
Q: Under the patronage of which Magadha king was the first Buddhist council held?
A: Ajatashatru (at Rajagriha).
Q: Under which king was the second Buddhist council held?
A: Kalashoka of the Sisunaga dynasty (at Vaishali).
Q: Who founded the Sisunaga dynasty?
A: Sisunaga, who overthrew the Haryanka rulers.
Q: Who was the founder of the Nanda dynasty?
A: Mahapadma Nanda.
Q: What is Mahapadma Nanda called in the Puranas?
A: 'Sarva Kshatrantaka' (destroyer of all Kshatriyas) and 'Ekarat' (sole sovereign).
Q: Which dynasty is described as the first non-Kshatriya dynasty of Magadha?
A: The Nanda dynasty.
Q: Who was the last ruler of the Nanda dynasty?
A: Dhana Nanda.
Q: Which Nanda ruler was a contemporary of Alexander?
A: Dhana Nanda.
Q: What was the capital of the Nandas?
A: Pataliputra.
Q: For what were the Nanda rulers famous?
A: Their enormous wealth and a huge standing army.
Q: Who overthrew Dhana Nanda and established the Maurya dynasty?
A: Chandragupta Maurya, with the help of Chanakya (Kautilya).
Q: Why was Rajagriha considered strategically important for Magadha?
A: It was surrounded by five hills that made it difficult to capture.
Q: Which period is known as the 'Second Urbanisation' of India?
A: The Mahajanapada period (6th century BC), marked by NBPW pottery and punch-marked coins.
Q: Which type of coins first appeared in the Mahajanapada period?
A: Punch-marked silver coins.
Q: Who invaded India in 326 BC?
A: Alexander the Great of Macedonia.
Q: Whom did Alexander defeat at the Battle of Hydaspes (Jhelum)?
A: King Porus (Puru).
Q: Which Mahajanapada lay in the Deccan with its capital at Paithan (Potana)?
A: Ashmaka.
Q: Which Mahajanapadas lay in the far north-west of India?
A: Gandhara and Kamboja.
Q: Which Mahajanapada had its capital at Ujjayini?
A: Avanti, with Ujjayini as its capital.
Q: Who founded the city of Pataliputra at the confluence of the Ganga and Son?
A: Ajatashatru, who built a fort at Pataligrama, later developed into Pataliputra.
Q: Is Mahajanapadas & Magadha Empire available for free on axomexam?
A: Yes. All questions, answers and explanations for Mahajanapadas & Magadha Empire are completely free, with no login or payment required.

A: Yes. Every question and answer in this topic is bilingual, so you can practise in Assamese and English.
