### Partition of Bengal & Swadeshi Movement | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/indian-history/modern-indian-history-sec/partition-bengal-swadeshi/
Summary: The partition of Bengal in 1905, the Swadeshi and Boycott movements, and the annulment of partition in 1911. Useful for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other Assam government exams.
Q: When was Bengal partitioned?
A: On 16 October 1905.
Q: Who was the Viceroy who partitioned Bengal?
A: Lord Curzon.
Q: What was the official reason given for the partition of Bengal?
A: To improve administrative efficiency, as the province of Bengal was too large.
Q: What was the real motive behind the partition of Bengal?
A: To weaken the rising national movement in Bengal by dividing the province on communal lines.
Q: Which two provinces were created by the partition of Bengal?
A: West Bengal (with its capital at Calcutta) and East Bengal and Assam (with its capital at Dacca).
Q: Who wrote the famous patriotic song 'Vande Mataram'?
A: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, in his novel Anandamath.
Q: What was the Swadeshi Movement?
A: A movement to promote Indian-made goods and boycott British goods.
Q: Who launched the Swadeshi Movement?
A: The movement was launched by the nationalists of Bengal in response to the partition, led by leaders like Surendranath Banerjee and Aurobindo Ghosh.
Q: What was the slogan of the Swadeshi Movement?
A: 'Vande Mataram'.
Q: Who was the leader who wrote the famous 'Sare Jahan Se Achha'?
A: Muhammad Iqbal, the poet.
Q: Who founded the 'Swadeshi Bandhav Samiti'?
A: Ashwini Kumar Dutta, at Barisal.
Q: Who wrote the book 'Swadeshi Andolan'?
A: No single author; it is a general topic. The main propagator of the idea was Aurobindo Ghosh and Bipin Chandra Pal.
Q: What was the 'Boycott Movement'?
A: The boycott of British goods as part of the Swadeshi movement.
Q: What was the main aim of the Swadeshi movement's boycott?
A: To hurt British economic interests and promote Indian industry.
Q: Who was the leader who called the partition of Bengal a 'settled fact'?
A: Lord Morley, the Secretary of State.
Q: When was the partition of Bengal annulled?
A: In December 1911, during the Delhi Durbar of George V.
Q: Who announced the annulment of the partition of Bengal?
A: Lord Hardinge, the Viceroy, at the Delhi Durbar.
Q: What was the capital of India shifted to in 1911?
A: From Calcutta to Delhi.
Q: Which new province was created in 1912 after the annulment?
A: Bihar and Orissa was separated from Bengal.
Q: What was the 'Rakhi Bandhan' day observed on 16 October 1905?
A: A day of protest observed by the Bengalis tying rakhis as a symbol of unity.
Q: Who was the leader who gave the slogan 'Swaraj is my birthright'?
A: Bal Gangadhar Tilak.
Q: What was the aim of the 'Anushilan Samiti' in the Swadeshi context?
A: To organise physical and revolutionary training for the youth.
Q: Who was the revolutionary who was the editor of 'Sandhya' and 'Yugantar'?
A: Braj Kishore Ghosh, and the Yugantar was edited by Bhupendranath Dutt and Barindra Kumar Ghosh.
Q: Who founded the 'Barisal Conference' of the Swadeshi movement?
A: Ashwini Kumar Dutta, which was held in 1906.
Q: What was the 'Lal-Bal-Pal' slogan referring to?
A: The trio of Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal.
Q: Who was the first president of the 'East Bengal and Assam' province?
A: The first Lieutenant Governor was J. Bamfylde Fuller.
Q: What was the attitude of the Assam valley towards the partition?
A: The Assam valley initially welcomed the partition as it was united with East Bengal, but later opposed it.
Q: Who was the leader of the anti-partition movement in Assam?
A: Leaders like Manik Chandra Baruah and others opposed the partition in Assam.
Q: What was the role of the press in the Swadeshi movement?
A: Newspapers like 'Kesari', 'Sandhya' and 'Yugantar' propagated the Swadeshi ideas.
Q: What was the 'Dacca Anushilan Samiti'?
A: A revolutionary organisation based in East Bengal, founded by Pulin Behari Das.
Q: Who was the famous leader who resigned from the 'Anushilan Samiti' to join the mainstream?
A: Aurobindo Ghosh moved towards spiritualism after the Alipore bomb case.
Q: What was the 'Alipore Bomb Case'?
A: The trial of the revolutionaries of the Anushilan Samiti after the attempt on the life of Kingsford in 1908.
Q: Who was the magistrate targeted by the revolutionaries in Muzaffarpur?
A: Kingsford, who was saved, but the bomb killed the two Barrister wives of Mrs. Kennedy.
Q: Who threw the bomb at Muzaffarpur?
A: Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki.
Q: Who was the revolutionary hanged in the Muzaffarpur case?
A: Khudiram Bose, who was only 18 years old.
Q: What was the 'Swadeshi' attitude towards the partition of Bengal by the Moderates?
A: The Moderates initially supported the protest but later differed on the boycott methods.
Q: Who was the Viceroy who succeeded Curzon?
A: Lord Minto.
Q: What was the 'Morley-Minto Reforms' of 1909?
A: The Indian Councils Act 1909, which introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
Q: What was the main drawback of the Morley-Minto Reforms?
A: The introduction of separate electorates for Muslims, which sowed the seeds of communalism.
Q: Who was the president of the INC at its Calcutta session of 1906?
A: Dadabhai Naoroji, the third time he presided.
Q: What was the main resolution passed at the Calcutta session of 1906?
A: The resolution supporting Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education.
Q: Who was the leader who founded the 'National Council of Education'?
A: The National Council of Education was founded in 1906 by the nationalists of Bengal, leading to the Jadavpur University.
Q: What was the 'Benaras session' of 1905 known for?
A: It was the session where G.K. Gokhale presided and the Congress condemned the partition.
Q: Who was the leader of the 'Swadeshi' movement who wrote 'Anandamath'?
A: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, though he wrote it before the movement, it inspired it.
Q: What was the role of Rabindranath Tagore in the Swadeshi movement?
A: He wrote patriotic songs and actively supported the movement, but later withdrew from it.
Q: Who was the leader who established the 'Bangabhanga' protest at the 'Hindu Mela'?
A: The Hindu Mela was founded earlier by Nabagopal Mitra; the protest against Bangabhanga was led by the nationalists.
Q: What was the result of the partition of Bengal on the national movement?
A: It gave a powerful impetus to the national movement and the rise of extremism.
Q: Who was the 'Bengal partition' annulled by which announcement?
A: The Royal Announcement by George V at the Delhi Durbar in December 1911.
Q: Which two leaders of the INC met Lord Minto in 1906?
A: Aga Khan and Gokhale discussed the Muslim demands, leading to separate electorates.
Q: What was the 'Swadeshi' movement's impact on the economy?
A: It promoted indigenous industries like textiles and banks, and reduced the demand for British goods.
Q: Who was the leader who started the 'Arya Samaj' in Assam during the Swadeshi period?
A: No major Arya Samaj was founded then; the social reform was led by figures like Gunabhiram Barua.
Q: What was the impact of the partition on the Assamese people?
A: The Assam valley was separated from the Brahmaputra valley's unity with Bengal, creating both benefits and grievances.
Q: Who was the leader who advocated the 'Boycott' of foreign goods as a political weapon?
A: Aurobindo Ghosh and Bipin Chandra Pal.
Q: What was the 'Jugantar Patrika'?
A: A revolutionary newspaper edited by Barindra Kumar Ghosh and Bhupendranath Dutt.
Q: Who was the leader who organised the 'Swadeshi mela'?
A: The first Swadeshi Mela was organised in 1901 by the Indian National Congress supporters in Bengal.
Q: When was Bengal partitioned?
A: On 16 October 1905, by Lord Curzon.
Q: Who partitioned Bengal?
A: Lord Curzon.
Q: What was the official reason given for the partition of Bengal?
A: Administrative efficiency, as Bengal was too large to be governed as one province.
Q: What was the real reason for the partition of Bengal?
A: To weaken the growing nationalism in Bengal by dividing the Bengalis.
Q: What was the Swadeshi Movement?
A: A movement to use Indian goods and boycott British goods, launched during the anti-partition agitation.
Q: What was the Boycott Movement?
A: The refusal to use British goods as part of the Swadeshi movement.
Q: Who were the leaders of the Swadeshi Movement?
A: Aurobindo Ghosh, Bipin Chandra Pal, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Lala Lajpat Rai.
Q: What was the national education movement?
A: The establishment of national schools and colleges as an alternative to government institutions during the Swadeshi period.
Q: Who founded the National Council of Education?
A: It was founded in 1906 in Bengal to promote national education.
Q: What was the 'Raksha Bandhan' protest during the anti-partition movement?
A: The tying of rakhis as a symbol of unity against the partition.
Q: When was the partition of Bengal annulled?
A: In December 1911, at the Delhi Durbar of King George V.
Q: Who announced the annulment of the partition of Bengal?
A: Viceroy Lord Hardinge, on behalf of King George V.
Q: When was the capital of British India shifted from Calcutta to Delhi?
A: In 1911.
Q: What was the impact of the Swadeshi movement on Indian industry?
A: It encouraged the growth of indigenous industries like cotton mills, soap, match and steel.
Q: What was the 'Vande Mataram'?
A: The patriotic song written by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, which became the anthem of the Swadeshi movement.

### Revolt of 1857 | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/indian-history/modern-indian-history-sec/revolt-of-1857/
Summary: The causes, course, leaders and results of the Revolt of 1857, the first major uprising against British rule. Covers ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: When did the Revolt of 1857 break out?
A: On 10 May 1857, at Meerut.
Q: Where did the Revolt of 1857 first break out?
A: Meerut.
Q: Who was the immediate cause of the Revolt of 1857?
A: The introduction of greased cartridges (rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat) which offended both Hindu and Muslim sepoys.
Q: Who was the first martyr of the Revolt of 1857?
A: Mangal Pandey, a sepoy of the 34th Native Infantry, who revolted at Barrackpore.
Q: Who proclaimed himself the leader of the Revolt of 1857 at Delhi?
A: Bahadur Shah II (Zafar), the last Mughal emperor.
Q: Who was the leader of the Revolt of 1857 in Kanpur?
A: Nana Saheb (Dhondu Pant), the adopted son of the last Peshwa Baji Rao II.
Q: Who was the leader of the Revolt of 1857 at Jhansi?
A: Rani Lakshmibai.
Q: Who was the leader of the Revolt of 1857 in Lucknow?
A: Begum Hazrat Mahal, the wife of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah.
Q: Who was the leader of the Revolt in Bihar (Arrah)?
A: Kunwar Singh, a zamindar of Jagdispur.
Q: Who was the leader of the Revolt of 1857 in Gwalior?
A: Tantia Tope, the general of Nana Saheb.
Q: Who was the ruler of Gwalior who supported the British during the Revolt?
A: Maharaja Scindia (Jayaji Rao Scindia).
Q: Which ruler of the Punjab helped the British in suppressing the Revolt?
A: The Sikhs under Maharaja Ranjit Singh's successors and the Punjab chiefs remained loyal to the British.
Q: Who was the Governor General of India at the time of the Revolt of 1857?
A: Lord Canning.
Q: Who was the commander-in-chief who suppressed the Revolt?
A: Sir Colin Campbell, and in Delhi, John Nicholson.
Q: Where was Bahadur Shah II exiled after the Revolt?
A: Rangoon (Yangon) in Burma.
Q: Who was the Nana Saheb in the Revolt of 1857?
A: Dhondu Pant, the adopted son of Baji Rao II, the last Peshwa.
Q: What was the main reason for the discontent of the sepoys?
A: The greased cartridges, poor pay and conditions, and the General Service Enlistment Act.
Q: What was the political cause of the Revolt of 1857?
A: The Doctrine of Lapse, the annexation of Awadh, and the abolition of pensions of rulers like the Peshwa.
Q: What was the social cause of the Revolt of 1857?
A: The fear of forced conversion to Christianity and the interference in social customs.
Q: What was the economic cause of the Revolt?
A: The heavy land revenue, the drain of wealth, and the destruction of Indian industries.
Q: Who was the leader of the Revolt in Bareilly?
A: Khan Bahadur Khan.
Q: Who was the leader of the Revolt in Allahabad?
A: Liaqat Ali.
Q: Who led the revolt in the Gorakhpur and Azamgarh regions?
A: Kunwar Singh and his brother Amar Singh.
Q: Who was the leader of the Revolt in Faizabad?
A: Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah, known as 'Danka Shah'.
Q: Who was the Mughal prince who fought against the British during the Revolt?
A: Mirza Mughal, son of Bahadur Shah II.
Q: What was the result of the Revolt of 1857?
A: The rule of the East India Company ended and India came under the direct rule of the British Crown.
Q: Which act transferred the government of India from the Company to the Crown?
A: The Government of India Act, 1858.
Q: Who was the first Viceroy of India?
A: Lord Canning.
Q: What was the 'Queen's Proclamation' of 1858?
A: The declaration by Queen Victoria promising no further annexation and religious tolerance.
Q: What happened to the Mughal dynasty after the Revolt?
A: The Mughal dynasty was abolished, and Bahadur Shah II was exiled to Rangoon.
Q: Which group of sepoys started the Revolt at Meerut?
A: The sepoys of the 3rd Cavalry, who were imprisoned and then released by their comrades.
Q: Why did the Revolt fail?
A: Lack of unity, no common programme, localised leadership, and the support of many Indian rulers and the modern educated class for the British.
Q: Which Indian states remained loyal to the British during the Revolt?
A: Hyderabad, Mysore, Gwalior (Scindia), the Punjab and the Rajput states.
Q: Who was the commander who recaptured Delhi?
A: The British forces under John Nicholson and General Wilson recaptured Delhi in September 1857.
Q: Who fought in the battle at Kotah ki Serai where Tantia Tope was defeated?
A: Tantia Tope was defeated by the British under Sir Hugh Rose.
Q: Who captured Jhansi from Rani Lakshmibai?
A: The British under Sir Hugh Rose, in April 1858.
Q: Where was Rani Lakshmibai killed?
A: At Gwalior, on 17 June 1858.
Q: Who was Tantia Tope's real name?
A: Ramachandra Pandurang Tope (also written as Tatya Tope).
Q: What was the result of the annexation of Awadh on the Revolt?
A: The annexation of Awadh alienated the taluqdars and led to a strong revolt in Awadh.
Q: Who was the leader of the Revolt in the 'Gorakhpur' region who was a zamindar?
A: Kunwar Singh.
Q: Which of the following was NOT a leader of the Revolt of 1857?
A: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, who was born much later (1856) and was not part of the Revolt.
Q: What was the British policy of 'Divide and Rule' after 1857?
A: The policy of creating divisions among Indians based on religion, caste and region to weaken the national movement.
Q: Which of the following was a result of the Revolt of 1857?
A: The end of the Company's rule, the abolition of the Doctrine of Lapse, and the reorganization of the army.
Q: What was the position of the princely states after 1858?
A: They were recognised as independent and were to remain loyal to the Crown.
Q: Who was the Secretary of State for India after 1858?
A: A member of the British cabinet who headed the India Office and was aided by the Council of India.
Q: What happened to the East India Company's army after 1857?
A: It was reorganised into the Indian Army under the British Crown.
Q: What was the immediate effect of the Revolt on the British attitude?
A: The British became suspicious of Indians and adopted a policy of racial discrimination.
Q: Who was the ruler of Delhi who was captured by the British?
A: Bahadur Shah II.
Q: What was the role of the Muslims in the Revolt?
A: Both Hindus and Muslims fought together against the British.
Q: Who was the leader of the revolt at 'Satara'?
A: The revolt at Satara was led by the followers of Nana Saheb and the deposed rulers.
Q: What was the condition of the peasants during the Revolt?
A: The peasants joined the Revolt due to the heavy revenue demands and the fear of losing their lands.
Q: Who was the British officer who killed Mangal Pandey?
A: Mangal Pandey was executed by the British after being captured; he was shot at Barrackpore.
Q: When did the Revolt of 1857 begin?
A: On 10 May 1857, at Meerut.
Q: Who was the leader of the revolt in Delhi?
A: Bahadur Shah Zafar (the last Mughal emperor).
Q: Who was the leader of the revolt in Kanpur?
A: Nana Saheb.
Q: Who was the leader of the revolt in Lucknow?
A: Begum Hazrat Mahal.
Q: Who was the leader of the revolt in Jhansi?
A: Rani Lakshmibai.
Q: Who was the leader of the revolt in Bareilly?
A: Khan Bahadur Khan.
Q: Who was the leader of the revolt in Bihar (Arrah)?
A: Kunwar Singh.
Q: What was the immediate cause of the Revolt of 1857?
A: The greased cartridges of the new Enfield rifles, which were rumoured to contain cow and pig fat.
Q: Who was the sepoy who refused to use the greased cartridges and was hanged?
A: Mangal Pandey, at Barrackpore in March 1857.
Q: Who was the Governor-General of India during the Revolt of 1857?
A: Lord Canning.
Q: Where did Rani Lakshmibai die?
A: In the battle of Gwalior, in June 1858.
Q: What was the Doctrine of Lapse?
A: A policy of annexing states whose rulers died without a natural heir, introduced by Lord Dalhousie.
Q: Which states were annexed by the Doctrine of Lapse?
A: Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, Sambalpur and Udaipur.
Q: What was the result of the Revolt of 1857?
A: The rule of the East India Company ended and India came under the direct rule of the British Crown.
Q: When was the Government of India Act 1858 passed?
A: In August 1858.
Q: Who became the first Viceroy of India?
A: Lord Canning.
Q: What happened to Bahadur Shah Zafar after the revolt?
A: He was exiled to Rangoon, where he died in 1862.
Q: What was the main cause of the failure of the Revolt of 1857?
A: Lack of unity, no common programme, and no support from many sections like the educated class and most princely states.
Q: Is Revolt of 1857 available for free on axomexam?
A: Yes. All questions, answers and explanations for Revolt of 1857 are completely free, with no login or payment required.
Q: Are the Revolt of 1857 questions available in Assamese as well as English?
A: Yes. Every question and answer in this topic is bilingual, so you can practise in Assamese and English.
Q: How many questions are there in this Revolt of 1857 question bank?
A: This page contains 70 practice questions, and new questions are added regularly.

### Revolutionary Freedom Movements | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/indian-history/modern-indian-history-sec/revolutionary-movements/
Summary: The revolutionary movements in Bengal, Maharashtra, Punjab and abroad - the Ghadar Party, the revolutionaries like Bhagat Singh, Chandrasekhar Azad and the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association. Covers ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: Who founded the Abhinav Bharat Society?
A: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar and his brother Ganesh Savarkar.
Q: Who founded the Ghadar Party?
A: Lala Har Dayal, in 1913 in San Francisco, USA.
Q: What was the newspaper of the Ghadar Party?
A: 'The Ghadar' (Gadar).
Q: Who founded the 'India House' in London?
A: Shyamji Krishna Varma.
Q: Who was the revolutionary who assassinated Curzon Wyllie?
A: Madan Lal Dhingra, in London in 1909.
Q: Who founded the 'Mitra Mela' which later became Abhinav Bharat?
A: The Savarkar brothers founded it in Nashik.
Q: Who was the leader of the 'Anushilan Samiti' in Calcutta?
A: Aurobindo Ghosh and Barindra Kumar Ghosh.
Q: Who was the founder of the 'Dacca Anushilan Samiti'?
A: Pulin Behari Das.
Q: Who founded the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA)?
A: Chandrasekhar Azad and Bhagat Singh, after the Kakori case.
Q: Who was the founder of the Hindustan Republican Association (HRA)?
A: Ram Prasad Bismil, Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee and Sachindra Nath Sanyal.
Q: What was the Kakori Conspiracy Case?
A: The robbery of a government train at Kakori (near Lucknow) in 1925 by the HRA to raise funds.
Q: Who was hanged in the Kakori Conspiracy Case?
A: Ram Prasad Bismil, Roshan Singh, Ashfaqullah Khan and Rajendra Lahiri.
Q: Who was the revolutionary who threw a bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly?
A: Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt, in 1929.
Q: Who was the British police officer killed by Bhagat Singh and his associates?
A: J.P. Saunders, in Lahore in 1928 (killed mistakenly for Scott).
Q: Why did Bhagat Singh and his comrades kill Saunders?
A: To avenge the death of Lala Lajpat Rai, who was injured in a lathi charge during the Simon Commission protest.
Q: Who was the leader who gave the slogan 'Inquilab Zindabad'?
A: Bhagat Singh popularised it, originally coined by Muhammad Iqbal.
Q: Who was the founder of the 'Naujawan Bharat Sabha'?
A: Bhagat Singh, in 1926 in Lahore.
Q: When were Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru hanged?
A: On 23 March 1931, at Lahore jail.
Q: Who was the revolutionary leader who escaped from the British and was known as 'Azad'?
A: Chandrasekhar Azad.
Q: Where did Chandrasekhar Azad die?
A: At Alfred Park in Allahabad, in 1931.
Q: Who led the Chittagong Armoury Raid?
A: Surya Sen (Masterda), in 1930.
Q: Who was the female revolutionary of the Chittagong raid?
A: Pritilata Waddedar, who led a raid on the European Club.
Q: Who was the revolutionary leader known as 'Masterda'?
A: Surya Sen.
Q: What was the 'Chittagong Armoury Raid'?
A: A raid on the armoury of Chittagong by revolutionaries led by Surya Sen in 1930 to seize arms.
Q: Who founded the 'India Independence League'?
A: Rash Behari Bose, in Japan.
Q: Who was the revolutionary who attempted to assassinate Lord Hardinge?
A: Rash Behari Bose, who threw a bomb at his procession in Delhi in 1912.
Q: Who was the revolutionary who planned the Delhi Conspiracy Case?
A: Rash Behari Bose and Sachin Sanyal.
Q: Who founded the 'Swadesh Bandhav Samiti'?
A: Ashwini Kumar Dutta.
Q: Who was the leader of the revolutionaries in the 'Sanyasi revolt'?
A: The Sannyasi revolt was a peasant uprising in Bengal; no single famous leader is recorded.
Q: Who was the revolutionary hanged in the 'Barisal conspiracy case'?
A: This was a trial of many revolutionaries; the prominent one was Trailokya Nath Chakravarty.
Q: Who was the leader of the 'Jugantar' group?
A: Barindra Kumar Ghosh and Aurobindo Ghosh.
Q: Who was the founder of the 'Anushilan' group in Mymensingh?
A: Hemendra Prasad Ghosh.
Q: What was the role of the revolutionaries in the Ghadar movement?
A: They tried to organise an armed rebellion in India with the help of the Indian soldiers abroad.
Q: What was the 'Komagata Maru' incident?
A: The ship carrying Indian immigrants that was prevented from landing in Canada in 1914, leading to violence.
Q: Who was the leader of the Komagata Maru?
A: Gurdit Singh.
Q: Who was the revolutionary who was a poet and wrote 'Sarfaroshi ki Tamanna'?
A: Ram Prasad Bismil.
Q: Who founded the 'Berlin Committee' during World War I?
A: Virendranath Chattopadhyay (Chatto), in 1914.
Q: Who was the founder of the 'Revolutionary Socialist Party'?
A: Ajoy Kumar Mukherjee, in 1940.
Q: Who was the revolutionary leader of the Punjab known as 'Master Tara Singh'?
A: Tara Singh was a Sikh leader, not a revolutionary of the armed kind; the Punjab revolutionary leader was Sohan Singh Josh (communist).
Q: Who was the founder of the 'Azad Hind Fauj' (INA) initially?
A: Mohammad Mohan Singh and later Subhas Chandra Bose took over its leadership.
Q: Who was the revolutionary woman who was a member of the 'Anushilan Samiti'?
A: Kalyani Das and later Bina Das, who shot at the Bengal Governor.
Q: Who shot at the Governor of Bengal in 1932?
A: Bina Das.
Q: Who was the leader of the revolutionaries in the 'Andaman Cellular Jail'?
A: Many revolutionaries like Barindra Ghosh, Sachin Sanyal and V.D. Savarkar were imprisoned there.
Q: Who was the revolutionary who wrote 'The Indian War of Independence'?
A: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar.
Q: What was the main objective of the revolutionary movements?
A: To achieve independence through armed struggle and to remove the British by force.
Q: Who was the revolutionary leader who was the editor of 'Pratap' newspaper?
A: Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi.
Q: Who founded the 'Hindustan Seva Dal'?
A: N.S. Hardikar, in 1923.
Q: Who was the revolutionary leader who died in the 'Lahore Conspiracy Case' trial?
A: The main martyrs were Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru.
Q: Who was the revolutionary who attempted to assassinate Sir John Simon?
A: The revolutionaries like Bhagat Singh's group; no direct attempt on Simon succeeded.
Q: Who was the leader of the 'All India Revolutionary Party'?
A: This is not a distinct well-known party; the main organisations were the HRA, HSRA, Ghadar and Anushilan.
Q: Who was the founder of the 'Anushilan Samiti'?
A: Pramathanath Mitra, in 1902 in Calcutta.
Q: Who was the leader of the 'Jugantar' party?
A: Barindra Kumar Ghosh.
Q: Who was the editor of the 'Jugantar' newspaper?
A: Bhupendranath Dutta.
Q: What was the Bengal Conspiracy Case?
A: The trial of the Alipore bomb case revolutionaries in 1908.
Q: Who was the defence lawyer in the Alipore Bomb Case?
A: Chittaranjan Das.
Q: Who was the revolutionary who escaped from the Alipore Jail?
A: Aurobindo Ghosh's brother Barindra Ghosh was imprisoned; the famous escape was of the revolutionary Upen Banerjee.
Q: Who was the founder of the 'Bharat Mata Society'?
A: Shyamji Krishna Varma.
Q: What was the 'India House'?
A: A hostel for Indian students in London that was a centre of revolutionary activity.
Q: Who founded the 'Free India Society'?
A: V.D. Savarkar, in London in 1907.
Q: Who was the founder of the 'Abhinav Bharat'? (English name)
A: It was called the 'Young India Society' in English.
Q: Who was the leader of the revolutionaries in the 1912 Delhi conspiracy?
A: Rash Behari Bose and Sachin Sanyal.
Q: Who was the founder of the 'Hindustan Ghadar' newspaper?
A: It was published by the Ghadar Party, led by Lala Har Dayal.
Q: What was the 'Mutiny of the Ghadar'?
A: The planned armed revolt in February 1915 by the Ghadar party with the help of Indian soldiers.
Q: Who was the leader of the Ghadar revolt of 1915?
A: Rash Behari Bose was the chief organiser.
Q: What was the 'Lahore Conspiracy Case' of 1915?
A: The trial of the Ghadar revolutionaries after the failed revolt of February 1915.
Q: Who was the revolutionary who killed a British officer in Poona in 1909?
A: Anant Lakshman Kanhere, who killed Collector Jackson.
Q: Who was the leader of the 'Anushilan Samiti' in Dacca?
A: Pulin Behari Das.
Q: Who was the founder of the 'Kirti' group in Punjab?
A: Bhagat Singh and Sukhdev, who started the 'Kirti Kisan' newspaper.
Q: Who was the leader of the 'Tarak Nath Das' group of revolutionaries?
A: Tarak Nath Das was a revolutionary who worked for the Ghadar movement from abroad.
Q: What was the significance of the revolutionary movement?
A: It inspired the youth and created a spirit of sacrifice, though it did not achieve immediate success.

### Socio-Religious Reform Movements | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/indian-history/modern-indian-history-sec/socio-religious-reforms/
Summary: The socio-religious reform movements of 19th century India - Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, Ramakrishna Mission, and the reformers like Raja Rammohan Roy, Dayananda and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar. Useful for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other Assam government exams.
Q: Who is regarded as the 'Father of Indian Renaissance'?
A: Raja Rammohan Roy.
Q: Who founded the Brahmo Samaj?
A: Raja Rammohan Roy, in 1828 AD.
Q: What was the main belief of the Brahmo Samaj?
A: Belief in one formless God and the rejection of idol worship, superstition and caste discrimination.
Q: Which reform was championed by Raja Rammohan Roy against Sati?
A: The abolition of Sati, which was legalised by Lord William Bentinck in 1829.
Q: Who was the Governor General who abolished Sati?
A: Lord William Bentinck, in 1829 AD.
Q: Who was the supporter of Rammohan Roy in the abolition of Sati?
A: His disciple William Carey and the support of Governor Bentinck.
Q: Who founded the Tattwabodhini Sabha?
A: Debendranath Tagore, in 1839 AD.
Q: Who was the leader of the Brahmo Samaj after Rammohan Roy?
A: Debendranath Tagore and later Keshab Chandra Sen.
Q: Who founded the breakaway 'Brahmo Samaj of India'?
A: Keshab Chandra Sen, in 1866 AD.
Q: Who was the founder of the Arya Samaj?
A: Swami Dayananda Saraswati, in 1875 AD.
Q: What was the motto of the Arya Samaj?
A: 'Back to the Vedas' and 'India for Indians'.
Q: Who founded the Dayanand Anglo-Vedic (DAV) schools?
A: The Arya Samaj after the death of Dayananda, following his vision of education.
Q: What was the Shuddhi movement of the Arya Samaj?
A: A movement to reconvert Hindus who had converted to other religions.
Q: Who wrote the book 'Satyarth Prakash'?
A: Swami Dayananda Saraswati.
Q: Who was the founder of the Ramakrishna Mission?
A: Swami Vivekananda, in 1897 AD.
Q: Who was the spiritual guru of Swami Vivekananda?
A: Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa.
Q: Where did Vivekananda deliver his famous speech on Hinduism?
A: At the Parliament of World Religions in Chicago in 1893 AD.
Q: Who founded the Theosophical Society in India?
A: Madam H.P. Blavatsky and Colonel H.S. Olcott, with headquarters at Adyar (Madras).
Q: Who was the president of the Theosophical Society who became a leading Indian nationalist?
A: Annie Besant.
Q: Who founded the Prarthana Samaj in Bombay?
A: Mahadev Govind Ranade and R.G. Bhandarkar.
Q: Who founded the Satya Shodhak Samaj?
A: Jyotirao Phule, in 1873 AD.
Q: What was the main aim of the Satya Shodhak Samaj?
A: To fight against caste oppression and the domination of the Brahmins.
Q: Who wrote 'Gulamgiri' (Slavery)?
A: Jyotirao Phule.
Q: Who was the wife of Jyotirao Phule who worked for women's education?
A: Savitribai Phule.
Q: Who founded the Widow Remarriage Association?
A: Vishnushastri Pandit, a reformer from Bombay.
Q: Who founded the Young Bengal movement?
A: Henry Louis Vivian Derozio, a teacher at Hindu College, Calcutta.
Q: What was the aim of the Young Bengal movement?
A: To promote rationalism, free thinking and social reform among the educated youth.
Q: Who was the founder of the Hindu College of Calcutta?
A: Raja Rammohan Roy, David Hare and others in 1817.
Q: Who was the great reformer of Bengal who fought for widow remarriage?
A: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.
Q: Which act legalised widow remarriage in 1856?
A: The Hindu Widow Remarriage Act, passed during the Governor Generalship of Lord Dalhousie.
Q: Who was the famous scholar who popularised the term 'Bande Mataram'?

Q: Who founded the Aligarh Movement?
A: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan.

Q: Who founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College?
A: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, in 1875 AD (later became Aligarh Muslim University).
Q: Who wrote the book 'Causes of Indian Revolt'?
A: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan.
Q: Who founded the Deoband movement?

Q: Who founded the Ramakrishna Mission's educational work?
A: Swami Vivekananda, who stressed on education for all, especially the poor.
Q: Who founded the Brahmo Samaj in Assam?

Q: Who was the first Assamese to write about widow remarriage?

A: Gopal Krishna Gokhale, in 1905 AD.
Q: Who founded the 'Bharat Stri Mahamandal'?
A: Sarala Devi Chaudhurani.

Q: Who founded the 'Sharada Sadan' for widows?
A: Pandita Ramabai.

Q: What was the main aim of the Brahmo Samaj?

A: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan.

### Subhas Chandra Bose and the Azad Hind Fauj (INA) | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/indian-history/modern-indian-history-sec/subhas-bose-ina/
Summary: The life of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose, the formation of the Indian National Army, its role in World War II and the Azad Hind Government. Covers ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: When and where was Subhas Chandra Bose born?
A: On 23 January 1897, in Cuttack, Odisha.
Q: What was the famous slogan of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose?
A: 'Delhi Chalo' (March to Delhi) and 'Jai Hind'.
Q: Who gave the slogan 'Jai Hind'?
A: Subhas Chandra Bose.
Q: What was the book written by Subhas Chandra Bose?
A: 'The Indian Struggle'.
Q: When was the first session of the Congress where Bose was elected as President?
A: In 1938, at the Haripura session.
Q: Who was Subhas Chandra Bose's rival in the 1939 Congress presidential election?
A: Pattabhi Sitaramayya (the Gandhian candidate).
Q: When did Subhas Chandra Bose escape from India?
A: In January 1941, from his house arrest in Calcutta.
Q: Who established the Free India Centre in Berlin?
A: Subhas Chandra Bose, in 1941.
Q: When was the Indian National Army (INA) formed?
A: In 1942, under the leadership of Mohan Singh in Singapore.
Q: Who was the founder of the Indian National Army?
A: Mohan Singh (with the support of Captain Fujiwara of Japan).
Q: Who took over the leadership of the INA from Mohan Singh?
A: Subhas Chandra Bose, in 1943.
Q: When did Subhas Chandra Bose arrive in Singapore?
A: In July 1943, by submarine.
Q: What was the name of the INA regiment of women?
A: The Rani of Jhansi Regiment, led by Lakshmi Swaminathan.
Q: Who was the leader of the Rani of Jhansi Regiment?
A: Captain Lakshmi Swaminathan (Lakshmi Sahgal).
Q: When was the Provisional Government of Free India (Azad Hind Government) formed?
A: On 21 October 1943, in Singapore.
Q: Where was the Azad Hind Government formed?
A: In Singapore.
Q: Who was the head of the Azad Hind Government?
A: Subhas Chandra Bose.
Q: Which country recognized the Azad Hind Government?
A: Japan, Germany, Italy and other Axis powers.
Q: What was the battle cry of the INA?
A: 'Delhi Chalo' (On to Delhi).
Q: Which islands were renamed by Subhas Chandra Bose?
A: Andaman and Nicobar islands were renamed 'Shahid' and 'Swaraj' islands.
Q: Who was the leader of the INA during the battle of Imphal and Kohima?
A: Subhas Chandra Bose led the INA in the invasion of India through Burma.
Q: What was the main aim of the INA?
A: To drive the British out of India with the help of the Axis powers.
Q: What was the strength of the INA under Bose?
A: About 60,000 soldiers, including many Indian prisoners of war.
Q: Where did the INA plant the national flag?
A: At Moirang in Manipur, on 14 April 1944.
Q: What was the INA war memorial called?
A: The 'Amar Jawan Jyoti' of the INA was the INA Martyrs' Memorial in Singapore.
Q: Where did Subhas Chandra Bose reportedly die?
A: In a plane crash at Taihoku (Taipei) on 18 August 1945.
Q: When did the INA trials begin?
A: In November 1945, at the Red Fort in Delhi.
Q: Who were the three officers tried first in the INA trials?
A: Prem Kumar Sehgal, Shah Nawaz Khan and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon.
Q: Who led the defence in the INA trials?
A: Bhulabhai Desai, with Tej Bahadur Sapru and Jawaharlal Nehru.
Q: What was the impact of the INA trials on India?
A: It created nationwide sympathy for the INA and hastened the British decision to leave India.
Q: What was the effect of the INA on the Royal Indian Navy Mutiny?
A: The INA trials inspired the naval ratings to mutiny in February 1946.
Q: What was the Royal Indian Navy Mutiny of 1946?
A: The revolt of naval ratings of the Royal Indian Navy in Bombay in February 1946.
Q: Which two slogans did the RIN mutiny raise?
A: 'Jai Hind' and 'Inquilab Zindabad'.
Q: Who was known as 'Netaji'?
A: Subhas Chandra Bose.
Q: What was the Indian Legion (Azad Hind Legion)?
A: The Indian soldiers recruited in Germany by Bose during World War II.
Q: What was the 'Azad Hind Radio'?
A: A radio station set up by Subhas Chandra Bose to broadcast his message to India.
Q: What did Bose say in his famous speech in Singapore in 1943?
A: He said 'Give me blood and I will give you freedom'.
Q: What was the Rani Jhansi Regiment?
A: The women's regiment of the INA formed in July 1943.
Q: Which fort was the site of the INA trials?
A: The Red Fort in Delhi.
Q: Who was the finance minister of the Azad Hind Government?
A: The prominent members included Subhas Chandra Bose as head and others like S.A. Ayer as publicity officer; the finance portfolio was held by Bose's close associates.
Q: What was the currency issued by the Azad Hind Government?
A: The Azad Hind Government issued its own currency notes.
Q: What was the battle for Imphal and Kohima?
A: The Japanese and INA offensive against the British in Manipur and Nagaland in 1944.
Q: Why did the INA fail in its march to Delhi?
A: Because of the failure of the Japanese supplies, monsoon floods and superior British forces.
Q: What happened to the INA soldiers after the war?
A: Many were captured, tried, and some were released after the INA trials.
Q: What was the contribution of the INA to India's freedom?
A: It exposed the loyalty of the Indian soldiers to the British and strengthened the demand for freedom.
Q: Who was Mohan Singh?
A: An Indian officer who founded the INA in 1942 in Malaya.
Q: What was the Bose's political philosophy called?
A: He advocated a synthesis of socialism and spiritualism, and radical revolution.
Q: When was Subhas Chandra Bose elected President of the Congress for the second time?
A: In 1939, at the Tripuri session, defeating Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
Q: What was the Forward Bloc?
A: A political party founded by Subhas Chandra Bose in 1939 after his resignation from the Congress.
Q: What was Netaji's famous war cry during the Azad Hind movement?
A: 'Chalo Delhi' (Onward to Delhi) and 'Tum mujhe khoon do, main tumhe azaadi dunga'.
Q: Where was Subhas Chandra Bose's father from?
A: His father Janakinath Bose was from Cuttack, Odisha.
Q: What was the name of Subhas Chandra Bose's wife?
A: Emilie Schenkl.
Q: What was Subhas Chandra Bose's daughter's name?
A: Anita Bose Pfaff.
Q: What did Subhas Chandra Bose call himself as the head of the Azad Hind Government?
A: The Head of State and Prime Minister of the Provisional Government of Free India.
Q: Which party did Subhas Chandra Bose form after leaving the Congress?
A: The Forward Bloc, in 1939.
Q: What was the 'Kadam Katar' slogan?
A: It is a phrase meaning 'I have decided to march forward'; it was a revolutionary slogan of the Azad Hind movement.
Q: Who was the commander of the INA at the time of the Moirang flag hoisting?
A: Shah Nawaz Khan's regiment planted the flag at Moirang.
Q: What was the 'Delhi Chalo' movement?
A: The INA's march towards Delhi to liberate India.
Q: Who was the propaganda officer of the Azad Hind Government?
A: S.A. Ayer.
Q: What was the 'Azad Hind Bank'?
A: A bank set up by the Azad Hind Government to manage its funds.
Q: What was the role of Japan in the INA?
A: Japan provided weapons, money and military support to the INA.
Q: Who was the leader of the INA's 'Rani of Jhansi' regiment?
A: Lakshmi Swaminathan (Lakshmi Sahgal).
Q: What was the outcome of the Imphal-Kohima campaign?
A: The INA and Japanese forces were defeated and forced to retreat.
Q: What happened to the INA after the surrender of Japan?
A: The INA was disbanded and many soldiers were captured and tried by the British.
Q: Who were the three INA officers tried in the first Red Fort trial?
A: Prem Kumar Sahgal, Shah Nawaz Khan and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon.
Q: What was the effect of the INA trials on the Indian public?
A: It created a wave of nationalist sentiment and protests across India.
Q: Who defended the INA officers in the Red Fort trial?
A: Bhulabhai Desai, assisted by Jawaharlal Nehru and Tej Bahadur Sapru.
Q: What was the impact of the INA on the British decision to leave India?
A: The INA trials and the naval mutiny convinced the British that they could no longer rely on Indian soldiers.
Q: What was the 'Azad Hind Radio' slogan?
A: 'Azad Hind' broadcast the message of freedom struggle to the Indian masses.
Q: What is the significance of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose in Indian history?
A: He was a great freedom fighter who built the INA and symbolised armed resistance to British rule.

A: Yes. Every question and answer in this topic is bilingual, so you can practise in Assamese and English.

### Article 371B & Assam Accord (Bilingual English & Assamese) | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/polity/assam-local-admin-sec/article-371b-assam-accord/
Summary: Article 371B & Assam Accord (Bilingual English & Assamese) - practice questions with answers for competitive exams in Assam. Covers ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, DME, SSC and Railway exams.
Q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution contains special provisions for Assam?
A: Article 371B.
Q: What does Article 371B of the Constitution provide for?
A: It provides for the constitution and functions of a committee of the Assam Legislative Assembly consisting of members elected from the tribal areas of the state.
Q: Who is empowered to make provisions under Article 371B for Assam?
A: The President of India.
Q: The committee under Article 371B consists of members elected from which areas of Assam?
A: The tribal areas of the state (the Sixth Schedule areas).
Q: What is the main purpose of Article 371B?
A: To protect the interests of the tribal areas within the Assam legislature.
Q: Which state's special provision is contained in Article 371A?
A: Nagaland.
Q: Which Article contains the special provision for Sikkim?
A: Article 371F.
Q: When was the Assam Accord signed?
A: On 15 August 1985.
Q: Where was the Assam Accord signed?
A: At Raj Bhavan, Guwahati.
Q: Between which parties was the Assam Accord signed?
A: Between the Government of India and the leaders of the Assam Agitation (AASU and AAGSP).
Q: Who represented the Government of India when the Assam Accord was signed?
A: Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi.
Q: Which organisations led the Assam Agitation?
A: The All Assam Students' Union (AASU) and the All Assam Gana Sangram Parishad (AAGSP).
Q: When was the Assam Agitation launched and how long did it last?
A: It was launched in 1979 and lasted until 1985 (1979-1985).
Q: Against what was the Assam Agitation launched?
A: Against illegal foreign (Bangladeshi) immigration into Assam.
Q: What is the cut-off date for the detection and deportation of foreigners under the Assam Accord?
A: 25 March 1971.
Q: Under the Accord, what was the status of those who entered India before 1966?
A: They were to be regularized.
Q: Under the Accord, what was to happen to those who entered India between 1966 and 25 March 1971?
A: Their names were to be deleted from the electoral rolls for 10 years and then restored.
Q: Under the Accord, what was to happen to those who entered India after 25 March 1971?
A: They were to be detected and deported.
Q: Which clause of the Assam Accord promises constitutional, legislative and administrative safeguards to protect the culture, language and identity of the Assamese people?
A: Clause 6.
Q: Which party came to power in Assam after the post-Accord elections?
A: The Asom Gana Parishad (AGP).
Q: When were the post-Accord elections held and who became Chief Minister?
A: In December 1985; Prafulla Kumar Mahanta.
Q: Who founded the Asom Gana Parishad (AGP)?
A: The leaders of the Assam Agitation (AASU).
Q: Under whose supervision was the National Register of Citizens (NRC) for Assam updated?
A: Under the supervision of the Supreme Court of India.
Q: When was the final NRC for Assam published?
A: In 2019.
Q: Was the Assam Accord signed during the Prime Ministership of Indira Gandhi?
A: No; it was signed on 15 August 1985 under Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi.

### Panchayati Raj & Municipalities (Bilingual English & Assamese) | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/polity/assam-local-admin-sec/panchayati-raj-municipalities/
Summary: Panchayati Raj & Municipalities (Bilingual English & Assamese) - practice questions with answers for competitive exams in Assam. Useful for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other Assam government exams.
Q: Which constitutional amendment act gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions?
A: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 (Part IX, Articles 243 to 243O).
Q: On which date did the 73rd Constitutional Amendment come into force, and which day is celebrated as National Panchayati Raj Day?
A: On 24 April 1993.
Q: Which committee recommended the three-tier Panchayati Raj system in 1957?
A: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee.
Q: In which state and district was Panchayati Raj first introduced on 2 October 1959?
A: In Rajasthan, at Nagaur.
Q: Which committee recommended a two-tier Panchayati Raj system in 1977?
A: The Ashok Mehta Committee.
Q: What is a Gram Sabha?
A: It is the assembly of all voters of a village.
Q: What is the fixed term of a Panchayat?
A: Five years.
Q: Who conducts elections to the Panchayats?
A: The State Election Commission.
Q: What is the minimum proportion of seats reserved for women in Panchayats?
A: At least one-third of the seats.
Q: How many subjects are listed in the 11th Schedule for Panchayats?
A: 29 subjects.
Q: Which Act of 1996 extended Panchayati Raj to the Scheduled Areas?
A: The PESA Act (Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act), 1996.
Q: Which Act provides for the three-tier Panchayati Raj system in Assam?
A: The Assam Panchayat Act, 1994.
Q: What are the three tiers of Panchayati Raj in Assam?
A: Gaon Panchayat (village), Anchalik Panchayat (block) and Zila Parishad (district).
Q: Which constitutional amendment act gave constitutional status to urban local bodies?
A: The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 (Part IXA, Articles 243P to 243ZG).
Q: What are the three types of urban local bodies under the 74th Amendment?
A: Nagar Panchayat (transitional area), Municipal Council (smaller urban area) and Municipal Corporation (larger urban area).
Q: Which type of urban local body is established for a transitional area?
A: Nagar Panchayat.
Q: How many subjects are listed in the 12th Schedule for municipalities?
A: 18 subjects.
Q: Which committees are provided in municipalities for each ward?
A: Wards Committees.
Q: Which is the only Municipal Corporation of Assam, constituted in 1971?
A: The Guwahati Municipal Corporation (GMC).
Q: The Guwahati Municipal Corporation is the municipal body of which city?
A: Guwahati, the capital city of Assam.
Q: Under which Part of the Constitution are the Panchayati Raj provisions (Articles 243 to 243O) found?
A: Part IX.
Q: Under which Part of the Constitution are the municipal provisions (Articles 243P to 243ZG) found?
A: Part IXA.
Q: Which amendment is related to urban local bodies (municipalities) and not to Panchayati Raj?
A: The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
Q: Which tier of Panchayati Raj in Assam is at the block (intermediate) level?
A: Anchalik Panchayat.
Q: What is the fixed term of a municipality under the 74th Amendment?
A: Five years.

### Sixth Schedule & Autonomous Councils in Assam (Bilingual English & Assamese) | axomexam

Q: What is the Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
A: It provides for the administration of certain tribal areas.
Q: Which Articles of the Constitution relate to the Sixth Schedule?
A: Articles 244(2) and 275(1).
Q: In how many states does the Sixth Schedule apply?
A: Four states.
Q: Name the four states to which the Sixth Schedule applies.
A: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
Q: What is the purpose of the Sixth Schedule?
A: To protect the interests of tribal people through the ADCs and ARCs.
Q: What do ADC and ARC stand for?
A: Autonomous District Council and Autonomous Regional Council.
Q: Which three types of powers do the ADCs possess?
A: Legislative, executive and judicial powers.
Q: Name any four subjects under the jurisdiction of the ADCs.
A: Land, forests, shifting cultivation and marriage (also village administration, inheritance and appointment of village chiefs).
Q: Do ADCs have jurisdiction over reserved forests?
A: No, reserved forests are excluded from their jurisdiction.
Q: Which three areas of Assam are covered under the Sixth Schedule?
A: Karbi Anglong, Dima Hasao and the Bodoland Territorial Area Districts (BTAD).
Q: Name the three autonomous councils of Assam under the Sixth Schedule.
A: Karbi Anglong Autonomous Council (KAAC), Dima Hasao Autonomous Council (DHAC) and Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC).
Q: What is the full form of KAAC?
A: Karbi Anglong Autonomous Council.
Q: What is the full form of DHAC?
A: Dima Hasao Autonomous Council.
Q: What was Dima Hasao district earlier known as?
A: North Cachar Hills district.
Q: In which year was the Bodoland Territorial Council established?
A: 2003.
Q: Under which Accord was the Bodoland Territorial Council created?
A: The Bodo Accord of 2003.
Q: Which organisation led the Bodoland movement?
A: The All Bodo Students' Union (ABSU).
Q: Who was the prominent leader of the Bodoland movement?
A: Upendra Nath Brahma.
Q: Under which legislation are councils like Deori, Mising and Tiwa constituted?
A: State (Assam) legislation, not the Sixth Schedule.
Q: Is the Rabha Hasong Autonomous Council under the Sixth Schedule?
A: No, it is constituted under an Assam state act.
Q: The Sixth Schedule does NOT apply to which of these states: Nagaland, Assam or Mizoram?
A: Nagaland.
Q: What is the full form of BTAD?
A: Bodoland Territorial Area Districts.
Q: What do the Sixth Schedule councils protect for the Scheduled Tribes?
A: Their interests and culture.
Q: Which is the most recently established among the three Sixth Schedule councils of Assam?
A: The Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC), established in 2003.
Q: Which body administers the tribal areas under the Sixth Schedule?
A: The Autonomous District Councils (ADCs).

### Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/polity/bodies-provisions-sec/cag/
Summary: Important questions on the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) for Assam competitive exams. Relevant for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other government exams.
Q: Under which Article of the Constitution is the Comptroller and Auditor General of India established?
A: Article 148.
Q: Who appoints the Comptroller and Auditor General of India?
A: The President of India.
Q: What is the main function of the CAG?
A: To audit the accounts of the Union Government, State Governments and public corporations.
Q: For how long does the CAG hold office?
A: Six years or till the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier.
Q: How can the CAG be removed?
A: In the same manner as a judge of the Supreme Court, i.e., by impeachment.
Q: Who administers the oath of office to the CAG?
A: The President of India.
Q: To whom does the CAG submit his report?
A: The President of India in respect of the Union, and the Governors in respect of the states.
Q: Which Committee of the Parliament examines the CAG report on the Union accounts?
A: The Public Accounts Committee (PAC).
Q: Who is the guardian of the public purse in India?
A: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India.
Q: What is the salary of the CAG?
A: It is equal to the salary of a judge of the Supreme Court.
Q: Who was the first Comptroller and Auditor General of India?
A: V. Narahari Rao.
Q: Is the CAG eligible for further government employment after his term?
A: No, he is not eligible for any further office under the Government of India or a state.
Q: Who audits the accounts of the State Governments?
A: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India.
Q: What is the constitutional status of the CAG?
A: It is an independent constitutional authority established under Article 148.
Q: What is the term of office of the CAG?
A: Six years from the date of assuming office, or till the age of 65, whichever is earlier.
Q: Can the CAG audit the accounts of local bodies?
A: Yes, he can audit the accounts of local bodies as well.
Q: Who presents the CAG report on state accounts in the State Legislature?
A: The Governor of the state.
Q: Which committee examines the CAG report in the State Legislature?
A: The Public Accounts Committee of the state.
Q: What are the three types of audit conducted by the CAG?
A: Financial audit, compliance audit and performance audit.
Q: Is the CAG a member of the Parliament?
A: No, the CAG is not a member of the Parliament.
Q: What is the role of the CAG in relation to the government companies?
A: He audits the accounts of government companies and corporations.
Q: Who is known as the 'Watchdog of the Public Purse'?
A: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India.
Q: What happens to the CAG report after it is submitted to the President?
A: It is laid before the Parliament for examination.
Q: Does the CAG require the consent of any authority to audit the government accounts?
A: No, the CAG can audit the accounts of the government on his own authority.
Q: Which Article empowers the CAG to audit the accounts of the states?
A: Article 149.

Q: Who appoints the Chief Election Commissioner of India?

Q: For how long does the Chief Election Commissioner hold office?

### Emergency Provisions (National, State and Financial Emergency) | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/polity/bodies-provisions-sec/emergency-provisions/
Summary: Important questions on the emergency provisions of the Indian Constitution for Assam competitive exams. Useful for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other Assam government exams.
Q: Under which Article can the National Emergency be declared?
A: Article 352.
Q: Who declares the National Emergency?
A: The President of India.
Q: On what grounds can the National Emergency be proclaimed?
A: War, external aggression or armed rebellion.
Q: Who must approve the proclamation of National Emergency?
A: Both Houses of Parliament, within one month of the proclamation.
Q: What is the maximum period for which the National Emergency can continue?
A: There is no maximum limit, but it must be approved by Parliament every six months.
Q: Which Fundamental Right is automatically suspended during the National Emergency?
A: The right to freedom of speech and expression (Article 19).
Q: Under which Article can the President impose President's Rule in a state?
A: Article 356.
Q: On what ground is President's Rule imposed in a state?
A: Failure of the constitutional machinery of the state.
Q: What is the maximum period for which President's Rule can be imposed in a state?
A: A maximum of three years, with parliamentary approval every six months.
Q: Who approves the proclamation of President's Rule?
A: Both Houses of Parliament.
Q: Under which Article can the Financial Emergency be proclaimed?
A: Article 360.
Q: On what ground can the Financial Emergency be proclaimed?
A: If the financial stability or credit of India or any part of its territory is threatened.
Q: Who proclaims the Financial Emergency?
A: The President of India.
Q: How many times has the National Emergency been declared in India so far?
A: Three times - 1962, 1971 and 1975.
Q: What was the ground for the National Emergency of 1975?
A: Internal disturbance (later changed to armed rebellion by the 44th Amendment).
Q: Which Amendment restricted the ground of National Emergency from 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion'?
A: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978.
Q: What is the effect of the National Emergency on Fundamental Rights?
A: Article 19 is suspended automatically, and other rights can be suspended by order.
Q: What happens to the State Government when President's Rule is imposed?
A: The state government is dismissed and the state is governed by the Governor on behalf of the President.
Q: Who approves the National Emergency when the Lok Sabha is dissolved?
A: The Rajya Sabha, within the specified period, and later the new Lok Sabha.
Q: What is the difference between the National Emergency and President's Rule?
A: National Emergency is declared for the whole country due to war or aggression, while President's Rule is imposed in a state due to constitutional failure.
Q: Who can revoke a proclamation of National Emergency?
A: The President, or the Lok Sabha by a resolution.
Q: What is the special majority required to approve a proclamation of emergency?
A: A majority of the total membership of each house and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.
Q: What happens to the life of the Lok Sabha during the National Emergency?
A: The term of the Lok Sabha can be extended beyond five years by Parliament, for one year at a time.
Q: Under which Article is the power to suspend Fundamental Rights during the National Emergency given?
A: Article 359.
Q: Which authority has the power to declare that a state is under President's Rule?
A: The President of India, on the report of the Governor or otherwise.

A: Yes. All questions, answers and explanations for Emergency Provisions (National, State and Financial Emergency) are completely free, with no login or payment required.

A: Yes. Every question and answer in this topic is bilingual, so you can practise in Assamese and English.

### Finance Commission and State Finance Commission | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/polity/bodies-provisions-sec/finance-commission-state-fc/
Summary: Important questions on the Finance Commission of India and the State Finance Commission for Assam competitive exams. Useful for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other Assam government exams.
Q: Under which Article of the Constitution is the Finance Commission established?
A: Article 280.
Q: Who appoints the Finance Commission of India?
A: The President of India.
Q: After how many years is the Finance Commission constituted?
A: Every five years.
Q: What is the main function of the Finance Commission?
A: To recommend the distribution of the net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the states.
Q: Who is the chairman of the Finance Commission?
A: A person appointed by the President, having experience in public affairs.
Q: What is the composition of the Finance Commission?
A: A Chairman and four other members.
Q: When was the first Finance Commission constituted?
A: In 1951.
Q: Who was the chairman of the first Finance Commission?
A: K.C. Neogy.
Q: Who was the chairman of the 15th Finance Commission?
A: N.K. Singh.
Q: What are the recommendations of the Finance Commission based on?
A: The population, income and fiscal needs of the states.
Q: Under which Article is the State Finance Commission established?
A: Article 243-I.
Q: Who appoints the State Finance Commission?
A: The Governor of the state.
Q: What is the main function of the State Finance Commission?
A: To recommend the distribution of financial resources between the state and the Panchayats and Municipalities.
Q: Who constitutes the State Finance Commission?
A: The Governor of the state.
Q: What is the composition of the State Finance Commission?
A: A Chairman and four other members, appointed by the Governor.
Q: How often is the State Finance Commission constituted?
A: Every five years.
Q: What are grants-in-aid?
A: Financial assistance given by the Union to the states, recommended by the Finance Commission.
Q: Which tax is divided between the Union and the states on the recommendation of the Finance Commission?
A: The shareable central taxes like income tax and excise duties (now GST).
Q: What is the devolution of taxes?
A: The transfer of a share of central taxes to the states as recommended by the Finance Commission.
Q: Who presents the recommendations of the Finance Commission to the Parliament?
A: The President of India, along with a memorandum explaining the action taken.
Q: What is the GST compensation fund?
A: A fund recommended to compensate states for any loss of revenue due to the implementation of GST.
Q: What is the period for which the Finance Commission makes its recommendations?
A: For a period of five years.
Q: Who has to implement the recommendations of the State Finance Commission?
A: The State Government, by presenting the recommendations to the State Legislature.
Q: What is the difference between the Finance Commission and the State Finance Commission?
A: The Finance Commission distributes taxes between the Union and the states, while the State Finance Commission distributes resources between the state and the local bodies.
Q: Which was the latest Finance Commission constituted for the period 2021-26?
A: The 15th Finance Commission.

### Citizenship - Indian Constitution (Bilingual English & Assamese) | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/polity/constitution-rights-sec/citizenship/
Summary: Citizenship - Indian Constitution (Bilingual English & Assamese) - practice questions with answers for competitive exams in Assam. Relevant for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other government exams.
Q: In which Part of the Indian Constitution are the provisions relating to citizenship found?
A: Part II (Articles 5 to 11).
Q: Which Articles of the Constitution deal with citizenship?
A: Articles 5 to 11.
Q: From which country's constitution did India adopt the idea of single citizenship?
A: Britain (British Constitution).
Q: What kind of citizenship does India provide?
A: Single citizenship.
Q: Which Article deals with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950)?
A: Article 5.
Q: Which Articles deal with the citizenship of migrants to India from Pakistan?
A: Articles 6 and 7.
Q: Which Article deals with the citizenship of persons of Indian origin residing outside India?
A: Article 8.
Q: Which Article says that a person who voluntarily acquires the citizenship of a foreign state shall not be a citizen of India?
A: Article 9.
Q: Which Article deals with the continuance of the rights of citizenship?
A: Article 10.
Q: Which Article gives Parliament the power to regulate the right of citizenship by law?
A: Article 11.
Q: Which Act governs the acquisition and termination of citizenship in India?
A: The Citizenship Act, 1955.
Q: What are the five ways of acquiring citizenship under the Citizenship Act, 1955?
A: By birth, by descent, by registration, by naturalisation, and by incorporation of territory.
Q: What are the three ways of losing citizenship under the Citizenship Act, 1955?
A: Renunciation, termination, and deprivation.
Q: When was the Citizenship Act first amended to restrict citizenship by birth?
A: In 1986.
Q: What condition did the 1986 amendment impose for citizenship by birth?
A: For those born on or after 1 July 1987, at least one parent must be an Indian citizen.
Q: What condition did the 2003 amendment impose for citizenship by birth?
A: For those born on or after 3 December 2004, both parents must be citizens, or one parent must be a citizen and the other not an illegal migrant.
Q: In which year was the Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) scheme introduced?
A: In 2005.
Q: Is OCI (Overseas Citizen of India) full citizenship of India?
A: No. OCIs cannot vote and cannot hold constitutional offices.
Q: Can an OCI (Overseas Citizen of India) holder vote in Indian elections?
A: No, OCI holders cannot vote.
Q: To which people does the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 grant citizenship?
A: Persecuted religious minorities - Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians - from Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan.
Q: What is the cut-off date fixed under the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019?
A: 31 December 2014.
Q: How many religious communities are covered by the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019?
A: Six - Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians.
Q: From how many countries does the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 cover migrants?
A: Three - Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan.
Q: What cut-off date was fixed by the Assam Accord (1985) for the detection and deportation of foreigners?
A: 25 March 1971.
Q: Who supervised the updating of the National Register of Citizens (NRC) in Assam?
A: The Supreme Court of India.

### Directive Principles & Fundamental Duties (Bilingual English & Assamese) | axomexam

Q: In which Part of the Constitution are the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) contained?
A: Part IV, Articles 36 to 51.
Q: From the Constitution of which country were the DPSP borrowed?
A: Ireland.
Q: Are the DPSP enforceable in a court of law?
A: No, they are non-justiciable (not enforceable by courts).
Q: Under Article 37, what is said about the DPSP?
A: They are 'fundamental in the governance of the country' and the State shall apply them while making laws.
Q: By what name are the DPSP often called?
A: 'Instrument of instructions' or 'a cheque on a bank payable at the convenience of the bank'.
Q: How are the DPSP classified?
A: Into Socialist Principles, Gandhian Principles, and Liberal-Intellectual Principles.
Q: Which Article deals with the welfare state and a just social order?
A: Article 38.
Q: Which Article provides for 'equal pay for equal work' for both men and women?
A: Article 39.
Q: Which Article provides for free legal aid to the poor?
A: Article 39A.
Q: Which Article provides for the organisation of village panchayats?
A: Article 40 (a Gandhian principle).
Q: Which Article deals with securing a living wage for workers?
A: Article 43.
Q: Which Article provides for the participation of workers in the management of industries?
A: Article 43A.
Q: Which Article deals with the Uniform Civil Code?
A: Article 44.
Q: Which Article provides for early childhood care and education of children below the age of 6 years?
A: Article 45 (as amended by the 86th Amendment).
Q: Which Article promotes the educational and economic interests of the SCs, STs and weaker sections?
A: Article 46.
Q: Which Article provides for the prohibition of intoxicating drinks?
A: Article 47.
Q: Which Article provides for the prohibition of the slaughter of cows and improvement of animal husbandry?
A: Article 48.
Q: Which Article deals with the protection and improvement of the environment?
A: Article 48A (added by the 42nd Amendment).
Q: Which Article provides for the separation of the judiciary from the executive?
A: Article 50.
Q: Which Article promotes international peace and security?
A: Article 51.
Q: What did the Supreme Court hold in the Minerva Mills case regarding the DPSP and Fundamental Rights?
A: Both are equally important and must be balanced; both form part of the basic structure of the Constitution.
Q: By which Constitutional Amendment Act were the Fundamental Duties added?
A: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.
Q: On whose recommendation were the Fundamental Duties added to the Constitution?
A: The Swaran Singh Committee.
Q: In which Part and Article are the Fundamental Duties contained?
A: Part IVA, Article 51A.
Q: Which Amendment added the 11th Fundamental Duty, and what is that duty?
A: The 86th Amendment (2002) - the duty of a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to their child or ward between 6 and 14 years.

Q: In which part of the Indian Constitution are the Fundamental Rights contained?
A: Part III (Articles 12 to 35).
Q: Which Article defines the 'State' for the purpose of Fundamental Rights?
A: Article 12.
Q: According to Article 13, what happens to any law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights?
A: It is void (judicial review).
Q: How many Fundamental Rights are there in the Indian Constitution?
A: Six.
Q: Which Articles deal with the Right to Equality?
A: Articles 14 to 18.
Q: Which Article guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws?
A: Article 14.
Q: Which Article prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth?
A: Article 15.
Q: Which Article provides equality of opportunity in matters of public employment?

Q: Which Article provides protection of life and personal liberty?
A: Article 21.
Q: Which Article provides the right to elementary education to children?

Q: Which Article provides protection against arrest and detention in certain cases?
A: Article 22.
Q: Which Articles deal with the Right against Exploitation?
A: Articles 23 and 24.
Q: Which Article prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour?

Q: Which Articles deal with the Right to Freedom of Religion?
A: Articles 25 to 28.
Q: Which Articles deal with Cultural and Educational Rights?
A: Articles 29 and 30.

A: Article 32.

Q: Which writ is issued to produce a person unlawfully detained before the court?
A: Habeas Corpus.

A: The 44th Amendment (1978); now under Article 300A.
Q: During a National Emergency, which two Fundamental Rights are never suspended?

### Historical Background, Making & Sources of Indian Constitution (Bilingual English & Assamese) | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/polity/constitution-rights-sec/historical-background-making-sources/
Summary: Historical Background, Making & Sources of Indian Constitution (Bilingual English & Assamese) - practice questions with answers for competitive exams in Assam. Relevant for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other government exams.
Q: Under which plan was the Constituent Assembly of India formed?
A: Under the Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946.
Q: When was the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly held?
A: On 9 December 1946.
Q: Who first put forward the idea of a Constituent Assembly for India?
A: M.N. Roy, in 1934.
Q: Who was the President of the Constituent Assembly?
A: Dr. Rajendra Prasad.
Q: Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
A: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
Q: How many members were there in the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
A: 7 members.
Q: Who moved the Objective Resolution in the Constituent Assembly and on which date?
A: Jawaharlal Nehru, on 13 December 1946.
Q: How much time did the Constituent Assembly take to frame the Indian Constitution?
A: 2 years, 11 months and 18 days.
Q: On which date was the Indian Constitution adopted?
A: On 26 November 1949.
Q: From which date did the Indian Constitution come into force?
A: From 26 January 1950.
Q: True or false: The Indian Constitution came into force on 26 November 1949.
A: False. It was adopted on 26 November 1949, but came into force on 26 January 1950.
Q: When was the draft Constitution submitted to the Constituent Assembly?
A: On 4 November 1948.
Q: Who was the Constitutional Advisor to the Constituent Assembly?
A: B.N. Rau.
Q: Why is the Indian Constitution called the longest written constitution and a 'bag of borrowings'?
A: Because it is the lengthiest written constitution in the world and has borrowed features from many constitutions of different countries.
Q: Which Act is the biggest source of the Indian Constitution?
A: The Government of India Act, 1935.
Q: Which features have been borrowed from the British Constitution?
A: Parliamentary system, rule of law, single citizenship, cabinet system, writs and legislative procedure.
Q: Which features have been borrowed from the US Constitution?
A: Fundamental Rights, independent judiciary, judicial review, impeachment of the President, removal of judges and the post of Vice-President.
Q: Which features have been borrowed from the Irish Constitution?
A: Directive Principles of State Policy, method of election of the President and nomination of members of the Rajya Sabha.
Q: Which features have been borrowed from the Canadian Constitution?
A: A strong centre in the federation, residuary powers with the Centre, appointment of state governors and advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
Q: Which features have been borrowed from the Australian Constitution?
A: The Concurrent List, freedom of trade and commerce and joint sitting of the two Houses of Parliament.
Q: From which constitution has the suspension of Fundamental Rights during emergency been borrowed?
A: From the German (Weimar) Constitution.
Q: From which constitution have the Fundamental Duties been borrowed?
A: From the Soviet (USSR) Constitution.
Q: From which constitution have the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity been borrowed?
A: From the French Constitution.
Q: From which constitution has the procedure of amendment been borrowed?
A: From the South African Constitution.
Q: How is India described in the Preamble of the Constitution?
A: As a 'Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic'.

### Preamble & Key Amendments of Indian Constitution (Bilingual English & Assamese) | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/polity/constitution-rights-sec/preamble-key-amendments/
Summary: Preamble & Key Amendments of Indian Constitution (Bilingual English & Assamese) - practice questions with answers for competitive exams in Assam.
Q: On which Resolution is the Preamble of the Indian Constitution based?
A: The 'Objective Resolution', moved by Jawaharlal Nehru.
Q: Who moved the Objective Resolution on which the Preamble is based?
A: Jawaharlal Nehru.
Q: What does the Preamble declare India to be?
A: A Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic.
Q: Which four ideals does the Preamble assure?
A: Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.
Q: What are the three forms of Justice assured by the Preamble?
A: Social, economic and political justice.
Q: What forms of Liberty does the Preamble assure?
A: Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.
Q: What does the Preamble assure under 'Fraternity'?
A: The dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation.
Q: By which Constitutional Amendment Act were the words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' added to the Preamble?
A: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.
Q: How many times has the Preamble of the Constitution been amended so far?
A: Only once, by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.
Q: Can the Preamble be enforced in a court of law?
A: No. The Preamble is non-justiciable.
Q: Which Constitutional Amendment Act is known as the 'Mini-Constitution'?
A: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.
Q: Which Constitutional Amendment added the Fundamental Duties (Article 51A)?
A: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.
Q: After the 86th Amendment (2002), how many Fundamental Duties are there in the Constitution?
A: 11 Fundamental Duties.
Q: Which Constitutional Amendment removed the Right to Property from the Fundamental Rights?
A: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978.
Q: After being removed from the Fundamental Rights, the Right to Property became a legal right under which Article?
A: Article 300A.
Q: Which Constitutional Amendment added the Anti-Defection Law (Tenth Schedule)?
A: The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985.
Q: Which Constitutional Amendment reduced the voting age from 21 years to 18 years?
A: The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1989.
Q: Which Constitutional Amendment gave constitutional status to the Panchayati Raj institutions?
A: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
Q: Which Constitutional Amendment gave constitutional status to the urban local bodies (Municipalities)?
A: The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
Q: Which Constitutional Amendment made elementary education a Fundamental Right (Article 21A)?
A: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002.
Q: For children of which age group does Article 21A provide free and compulsory elementary education?
A: Children aged 6 to 14 years.
Q: Which Constitutional Amendment introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST)?
A: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016.
Q: Which Constitutional Amendment provided 10% reservation for the Economically Weaker Sections (EWS)?
A: The 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019.
Q: Which Constitutional Amendment provided 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies?
A: The 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023.
Q: TRUE or FALSE: The words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added to the Preamble by the 44th Amendment (1978).
A: False. They were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

### Judiciary: Supreme Court, High Courts and Subordinate Courts | axomexam
URL: https://axomexam.in/topic/gk/polity/union-state-governance-sec/judiciary-supreme-court-high-courts-subordinate/
Summary: Important questions on the Supreme Court, High Courts and Subordinate Courts for Assam competitive exams. Relevant for ADRE, APSC, Assam Police, DHS, SSC, Railway and other government exams.
Q: Which is the apex court of India?
A: The Supreme Court of India.
Q: Under which Article of the Constitution is the Supreme Court established?
A: Article 124.
Q: Who appoints the judges of the Supreme Court?
A: The President of India.
Q: What is the retirement age of a judge of the Supreme Court?
A: 65 years.
Q: Who is the head of the Supreme Court of India?
A: The Chief Justice of India (CJI).
Q: What is the present sanctioned strength of the judges of the Supreme Court?
A: 34 (including the Chief Justice of India).
Q: What is the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court?
A: It can hear disputes between the Government of India and the states, and between states.
Q: What is a writ?
A: A formal written order of a court directing a person or authority to do or refrain from doing something.
Q: How many types of writs can the Supreme Court issue?
A: Five - Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Certiorari, Prohibition and Quo Warranto.
Q: Which writ is issued to produce a person who has been detained in custody?
A: Habeas Corpus.
Q: Which writ is issued to a public official to perform his duty?
A: Mandamus.
Q: Which writ is issued to quash an order of a lower court or tribunal?
A: Certiorari.
Q: Which writ is issued to prevent a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction?
A: Prohibition.
Q: Which writ is issued to question a person's right to hold a public office?
A: Quo Warranto.
Q: Under which Article can the President seek the advisory opinion of the Supreme Court?
A: Article 143.
Q: What is judicial review?
A: The power of the courts to examine the constitutionality of laws passed by the legislature.
Q: Under which Article is the High Court of a state established?
A: Article 214.
Q: What is the retirement age of a judge of a High Court?
A: 62 years.
Q: Who appoints the Chief Justice of a High Court?
A: The President of India.
Q: Who appoints the judges of a High Court?
A: The President of India, in consultation with the Chief Justice of India and the Governor of the state.
Q: Which is the highest court of a state?
A: The High Court.
Q: What are the subordinate courts?
A: The district courts and the courts below them, functioning under the High Court.
Q: Who appoints the District Judge?
A: The Governor of the state, in consultation with the High Court.
Q: Under which Article is the district court established?
A: Article 233.
Q: What is the advisory jurisdiction of the High Court?
A: The High Court can give its opinion on a question of law referred by the Governor.
